# TO THE MOST SERENE AND MOST POWER-
## ful Lord, Lord Edward, the sixth of that name, King of England,
## France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, etc. Ni-
### colaus Pruckner sends greetings. <note>original: "S. D." for Salutem Dicit</note>

---

<image-desc>A large square woodcut initial letter 'A'. Inside the letter frame, two men in 16th-century scholarly attire are depicted. The figure on the left holds an armillary sphere or celestial globe. The figure on the right is seated at a desk, using a pair of dividers or a compass to measure a large triangular diagram. The scene is set within an architectural interior.</image-desc>
**ANCIENT** is the division of <term>Astrology</term> <note>In the 16th century, "Astrology" encompassed both what we now call astronomy (the math of stars) and astrology (their influence).</note> handed down by Ptolemy, King Edward: one part of it belongs to **knowledge and contemplation**, and is free and clear from all criticism. The other part belongs to **action**, and has been attempted even by the rebukes of great men. For the first part, as if penetrating the heavens with wisdom, explains its spheres, various motions, the courses of the stars, their magnitudes, and their differences in such a way that it leaves no doubt or hesitation. From this we understand the eclipses of the Sun and Moon; from this, the rising and setting of the stars; from this, the measured journeys of the seven wandering stars <note>The "planets" known to the ancient world: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon.</note>, which can be noted and marked for many centuries in advance, down to the very moments and points of time. Because that part has been explored and is always free from error, it is believed to be the leader of this doctrine.

The other part is most criticized for the very reason it ought to be most celebrated: namely, because of the **ignorance of the common people**, even though it has always been most useful and often even life-saving for the needs of men and the conduct of life—if, like that other part, it were mastered by its teachers. But arts are not to be blamed because they are unknown; rather, because there are few who attain them, he who does attain them ought to be praised most highly. Because such knowledge is rare, the genius of the craftsman must be considered singular. 

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that there is a large crowd of people professing this art, and many more practice this latter part before they have learned the former. In this study, there are two chief vices. Because they do not perfectly master that first part, being content with the discoveries of others, they discover nothing themselves; then, they generally use those very things which they received from others poorly and without understanding. From this, two great vices are born: one of **laziness**, the other of **stupidity**. But this class of men would not be much of an obstacle to the reputation of the art, were it not that some learned men, and among them even some good men, have also stood forth as critics of this science. To them I briefly respond: Arts are not blameworthy because they are unknown; rather, it is fitting they be held in high esteem because there are few who can master them. Nor should this part of Astrology be rebuked because Ptolemy held it with only a few others; rather, it is all the more wonderful and divine the fewer mortals to whom it has been granted. 

Who can deny that if the motions of the heavens are certain and their actions defined, something certain is also produced by them? So that even if events seem to happen to men by chance, a wise man will understand that they occur and happen, as it were, through knowledge. Who does not see that the bodies of living creatures are filled, emptied, weakened, or strengthened according to the <term>constitution of the Moon</term>? Even the Ocean itself is governed by the command of this light. If people require authority, what do the ancient names of the stars and signs signify...

<summary>In this dedication to King Edward VI, Nicolaus Pruckner defends astrology by distinguishing between its "certain" mathematical side (astronomy) and its predictive side, arguing that the latter is a divine but difficult science often tarnished by unskilled practitioners.</summary>
<keywords>Edward VI, Ptolemy, astrology vs astronomy, celestial influence, scientific defense, 16th-century science</keywords>

<meta>The previous page's catchword "ximus" likely completed a word like "maximus" (greatest) or "proximus" (nearest). This page continues the argument for astrology by citing ancient poets and philosophers to show that the stars have always been understood to influence earthly life.</meta>

### PREFACE.

...and the ancient names of the Pleiades and the Hyades <note>Two prominent star clusters in the constellation Taurus, often associated with rain in antiquity.</note>; and why was Orion called "watery" by the most ancient poets? Why is Sirius called "burning"? Who is unaware that at its rising the heat of the Sun is kindled? <note>original: "λαμπρότατος μ' ὅγ' ἐστὶ, κακὸν δέ τι σῆμα τέτυκται, καί τε φέρει πολλὰν πυρετὸν δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν." This is a quote from Homer's *Iliad* (22.30-31), describing the star Sirius: "He is the brightest, but he is wrought as an evil sign, and brings much fever to wretched mortals."</note> For the effects of that star are most greatly felt upon the earth. Why have the seasonal patterns for days, throughout all months and the entire year, been noted by writers because of the rising and setting of the stars? Is Aristotle not a great enough authority, who even in his *Politics* admits that by the temperate nature of the Sun, not only bodies but also human minds are governed? Is it for nothing that Cicero called the brightness of Jupiter prosperous and healthy for the human race? And before Cicero, Plautus speaks thus concerning the star Arcturus, and both its influence and its effect:
> I am Arcturus, the sharpest of all signs:
> I am fierce when rising, and fiercer still when I set.

Therefore, among the Romans, this art flourished not only in the later times of that Empire, but even among the first people, to whom this art was spread from Greece and <term>Chaldea</term> <note>An ancient region in Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) whose people were famed as the founders of astronomy and astrology.</note>; for the Greek books on this science are older and more numerous. The most ancient writer is Aratus; and he says of this method:
> <note>original: "Μόχθος μέν τ' ὀλίγος, τὸ δὲ μυρίον αὐτίκ' ὄνειαρ Γίνετ' ἐπιφροσύνης αἰεὶ πεφυλαγμένω ἀνδρί." From Aratus's *Phaenomena*: "The labor is small, but the benefit is immediately vast for the man who is always guarded by wisdom."</note>

But yet it is true in this discipline, as is said in the proverb, "It does not happen to everyone to go to Corinth." <note>A common Latin proverb (*Non omnibus contingit adire Corinthum*) meaning that difficult or expensive goals are not attainable by everyone.</note> There are few who attain it: first, because it requires a great sharpness of mind, great industry, and learning; then because many and great things still lie hidden within it,
> <note>original: "πάντα γὰρ οὔπω Εκ Διὸς ἄνθρωποι γιγνώσκομεν, ἀλλ' ἔτι πολλὰ κέκρυπται." Also from Aratus: "For we humans do not yet know all things from Zeus, but much is still hidden."</note>
Many things have also been discovered which, if not properly applied, bring about great errors. Proclus was a noble interpreter of Plato and a distinguished man in natural philosophy; he writes most truly that <note>original: "ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ τοῦ λέοντος κείμενος λαμπρὸς ἀστὴρ... βασιλικὸν ἔχειν τὸ γενέθλιον." Translation: "The bright star situated at the heart of the Lion is called, according to the place where it lies, the 'Heart of the Lion.' By some it is called 'the little king' [Basiliskos], because those born when the Sun is in this place are known to have a royal birth."</note> All this is true. For there is a star in that place which is named the <term>Heart of the Lion</term> <note>Latin: *Cor leonis*.</note>, and *Basililicus*, as if it were <term>Regulus</term> <note>The star Regulus; the name means "Little King."</note>: and those who have their birth with this star seem to be born to a royal condition. For as that man says,
> <note>original: "Ἀστήρ ἀνθρώποισι τετυγμένα σημαίνουσι." Translation: "The stars signify the things ordained for men."</note>
But because it seems all [born then] share this fortune, it is not certain who they truly are, except to perceptive and learned men who can note the exact moments of time, who can skillfully distinguish the spaces of the heavens and the twelve houses <note>The "houses" are the twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in a horoscope.</note>, who can observe the arrangements of the other stars, and with these, can skillfully compare the one about whom a judgment is to be made: something which many ancients achieved. For since we have said enough about authority for now, we must now come to examples; if we bring some of these forward, it will be demonstrated by us that this art exists, that there have been practitioners of it, and that it can be understood. Valerius Ma- <note>This likely refers to Valerius Maximus, a Roman author of historical anecdotes.</note>

<summary>Pruckner defends astrology by citing classical authorities like Homer, Aristotle, and Cicero, arguing that celestial bodies exert a physical and spiritual influence on Earth. He highlights the star Regulus as a prime example of how specific stars indicate a person's destiny, though he warns that interpreting these signs requires deep expertise.</summary>

# PREFACE.

α 3

...[Valerius Ma]ximus, a far-sighted writer of history, records that when Aeschylus <note>A famous Greek tragic playwright (c. 525–456 BC).</note> received an answer from the <term>Mathematicians</term> <note>In this period, "mathematician" (mathematicus) was the standard term for an astrologer.</note> that he was destined to die from a blow falling from a high place, he avoided buildings and remained under the open sky with his head uncovered. However, an eagle dropped a tortoise upon him, and he died from that accident; thus, the prediction proved to be true. Who among the Roman emperors was considered more fortunate than Augustus? On his silver coins was the image of Capricorn, the sign of both his star and his fortune, which Theogenes had foretold. After learning the diagram of Augustus's birth and origin, Theogenes had fallen down and worshipped him. Augustus, moved by Theogenes's foresight, confirmed this prediction on his own coinage by marking the money with the sign of Capricorn. 

The <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>A term often used in antiquity to refer to Babylonian astrologers or experts in the occult sciences.</note> answered Agrippina, the mother of Nero, that her son would be emperor, but also a parricide who would cause his mother’s death. She replied, "Let him kill me, provided that he rules." And indeed, he did rule, and he did kill his mother. Sulla the Mathematician had foretold the approaching death of Caligula. Vespasian granted so much credit to this art that, amidst constant conspiracies against him, he dared to assert that either his sons would be his successors in the empire, or no one would. 

When Domitian was a young man, the Chaldeans indicated the day, the hour, and the manner of his death. When this prophecy was brought up during the trial of Ascletarion the Mathematician—who had been charged with a capital crime—Domitian, wishing to test the man's skill, asked Ascletarion if he knew by what kind of death he himself was destined to perish. He replied that he would soon be torn apart by dogs. Domitian, hoping to prove the <term>genethliac</term> <note>An astrologer who casts birth charts (genethlialogy).</note> prophet a liar, immediately ordered him to be executed and his corpse to be buried with the utmost care. But a storm suddenly arose, the funeral pyre was scattered, and dogs tore apart the scorched body. 

The Emperor Hadrian, because he was highly skilled in this art and teaching, wrote down for himself every year what would happen each day. His uncle, Aelius Hadrianus, had predicted the empire for him using this art, and Hadrian learned the same from another mathematician before he took power. It is also well known that he often said of Verus:

->The fates will only show this man to the earth,<-
->nor will they allow him to remain longer.<-
<note>original: "Ostendent terris hunc tantum fata, neque ultrà / Esse sinent." This is a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.869-870).</note>

I could bring forward many examples from our own age, and I could even mention things I have predicted for leading men, if both were not likely to cause offense. Antiquity is far removed from such jealousy. Even if no other example existed except that of the Magi, who saw the star of Christ in the East, it would still be a great argument that momentous events are signaled to men by the stars—whether by their eternal motion or by some divine decree—not to all people, but to those who are certain and knowledgeable. 

These are the things I wished to say to you in this preface, King Edward <note>King Edward VI of England (reigned 1547–1553).</note>, on behalf of Julius Maternus Firmicus <note>A 4th-century Roman lawyer and author of the *Mathesis*, a major Latin work on astrology.</note>, an ancient, pure, and approved writer of this art, whose work is now corrected; and on behalf of this art itself, against the many slanders it has suffered. One such slander is that the Mathematicians were expelled from the city by Tiberius Caesar—as if the same had not also happened to the Rhetoricians in that same city of Rome. Plato excluded poets from his Republic; is the art of poets therefore inherently ruinous, even if there are many bad poets? Still, Plato's judgment is very grave, I admit. But no one contributed more to the death of Socrates than the poet Aristophanes. Therefore...

<meta>The catchword "tior" at the bottom of the page likely connects to "patior" (to suffer) or "potior" (to obtain) on the following leaf.</meta>

He defends the study of astrology to King Edward VI, arguing that the failures of individual practitioners do not invalidate the entire science.</summary>

# PREFACE.

...[more worthy of note], that Plato hated Aristophanes; however, I do not approve of the fact that he also hated even good poets. Arts and virtues must be valued as they are in themselves, not by their outcome, nor by the wickedness of men. Otherwise, both prophets and apostles would have to be cast out from the state, since all of them were either slaughtered or treated poorly. And these past two years have cast many good Evangelical preachers <note>The author uses the term "Ecclesiastes Euangelicos," referring to the Protestant reformers and preachers who were often exiled during the religious upheavals of the mid-16th century.</note> out of cities; is the Gospel therefore not true, or are they therefore evil? This is the <term>testing</term> <note>Original: *dokimasia* (δοκιμασία). In ancient Athens, this was a formal investigation into a person's character and eligibility for public office.</note> of goodness: to be driven out by one's own people and to be called upon by foreigners; to suffer while living, but to be celebrated when dead. 

Indeed, this youthful virtue of yours, O King, is being tested no small amount, together with the rebirth of religion in that kingdom: are you therefore not worthy to rule? Let vices roar as they will; your virtue—as all good men hope and trust—your innate character of virtue, religion, and goodness, I say, will mature and grow

->into Royal Majesty, the enlargement of the kingdom, the<-
->confirmation of religion, toward peace, toward tranquility,<-
->toward the salvation of the people. Farewell. Strasbourg.<-
->28 January. In the year from the birth of<-
->Christ 1551.<-

# ON THE DEFINITIONS AND TERMS 
## OF ASTROLOGY, A BOOKLET BY OTTO
->Brunfels.<-

**Astrology** is the knowledge of the actions and significations of the stars and the heavens; in Latin, it is called the "sidereal science."
**Dioptics**, a part of Astrology, investigates the distances of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars using instruments.
**Meteoroscope**, a part of Astrology, searches for the differences in elevations and the distances of the stars.
**Gnomonics**, a part of Astrology, teaches the theory of shadows and sundials, and does so by means of a "spit" or **gnomon** <note>A gnomon is the vertical rod or part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>.
**Astron**, according to Macrobius <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman provincial and author famous for his commentary on the 'Dream of Scipio,' which was a standard textbook for medieval astronomy.</note>, refers to a single star.
**Astron** also refers to a "sign" composed of stars, which we call a **constellation** <note>Original: *sidus*</note>. Thus, there are "singular stars," such as the five "Wandering Stars" <note>The planets: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note> and others that travel alone without being mixed with others.
**Constellations** <note>Original: *Sidera*</note>, however, are those formed by a composition of several stars into a specific sign, such as Aries, Taurus, Andromeda, Perseus, the Crown, and whatever types of various forms are believed to have been received into the heavens.
**Horoscope** <note>In this period, 'Horoscope' refers specifically to the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, known today as the Ascendant.</note> is the sign which is ascending.

->NAMES OF THE PLANETS<-
->Greek.<-

♄ The Shining One <note>Greek: *Phainon* (Φαίνων)</note>. ♃ The Radiant One <note>Greek: *Phaethon* (Φαέθων)</note>. ♂ The Fiery One <note>Greek: *Pyroeis* (Πυρόεις)</note>.
☉ The Sun <note>Greek: *Helios* (Ἠέλιος)</note>. ♀ The Light-Bringer <note>Greek: *Phosphoros* (Φωσφόρος)</note>. ☿ The Gleaming One <note>Greek: *Stilbon* (Στίλβων)</note>.
☽ The Moon <note>Greek: *Selene* (σελήνη)</note>.

**Altitude** <note>Often called 'Exaltation' in modern astrology.</note> of the planets is so named because when stars are positioned in that specific part, they make men blessed, or it is when they are raised up by a certain natural sublimity of greatness.
**Dejected** <note>Original: *Deiecti*. In modern terms, 'Fall.' This occurs in the sign opposite the planet's exaltation.</note> planets are so named when their authority is suppressed; they make men wretched, poor, ignoble, and destitute.
**Zodegoi** <note>Original Greek: ζωδηγοι. This refers to the 'life-givers' or 'lords' of the signs.</note>, or "benefactors," are triple powers applied to each of the **decans** <note>A decan is a 10-degree segment of a zodiac sign; there are 36 in total.</note>. Concerning these, see Firmicus <note>Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman lawyer and astrologer who wrote the 'Mathesis,' one of the most complete handbooks of ancient astrology.</note> in book two, chapter four.
**Terms** of the stars are what the specific parts of the signs are called, which are divided among the individual stars; in Greek, they are called the *oria* <note>Original: τὰ ὅρια. 'Terms' (fines) are specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign ruled by different planets.</note>.
Planets are said to **rejoice** when, in a birth chart, they are positioned in favorable and more fortunate places, where they have greater power and decree a great deal of good fortune.
There are five **morning stars**: ♄, ♃, ♂, ♀, and ☿. These same stars are also called **evening stars**, **western stars**, and **hidden stars**. In Greek: *aphanitoi*, *synodikoi*, and *akronyctoi* <note>Original: ἀφανίτοι καὶ συνοδικοί καὶ ἀκρονύκτοι. These terms describe the planet's relationship to the Sun—whether they are invisible, meeting the Sun, or rising at sunset.</note>.
A **morning star** is what a star is called when, existing at its rising,

<column-break/>

it precedes the Sun <note>Original: ☉</note> from the east, such as **Lucifer** <note>The Latin name for Venus when it appears as the morning star, meaning 'Light-Bringer.'</note>.
An **evening star** is one which, at its rising, follows the rising Sun.
**Hidden stars** are those which the orb of the Sun covers <note>This refers to 'combustion,' when a planet is too close to the Sun to be seen.</note>.
**Akronyctoi** <note>Original: Ακρονύκτοι</note> are those which rise just as the Sun verges toward its setting.
Stars are said to be **protected** whenever they precede the Sun with a favorable radiation.
The power of the Sun is protected by the best radiation whenever it is adorned by the morning rising of the stars.
**Saturn** is called "morning" when it precedes the Sun by twelve degrees.
**Jupiter** is "morning" when it has moved away by preceding the Sun by eleven degrees.
**Mars**, preceding the Sun by eight degrees, is called "morning."
Likewise, **Venus**, when positioned in the eighth degree <note>meaning 8 degrees from the Sun</note>, is called "morning."
**Aries** is called a **tropic sign** <note>The Latin 'tropicus' here refers to a 'turning point,' specifically the Spring Equinox.</note> because, when the Sun is positioned in that sign, it creates the springtime.
Aries is called a **fiery sign** because whoever has it in the horoscope of their birth chart will be prone to fire and a **choleric nature** <note>In the four humors theory, the choleric temperament was associated with fire, heat, and irritability.</note>.
**Platica** <note>Likely from the Greek 'platikos,' meaning 'wide.' Here it refers to the 'place of life' (Hyleg) associated with the Ascendant's sign.</note> is the place of life in that sign in which the horoscope is established.
**Anatole** <note>Original: ἀνατολή</note>: the eastern angle, the first house.
**Dysis** <note>Original: δύσις</note>: the west.
**Mesouranion** <note>Original: μεσουράνιον</note>: the mid-heaven <note>The highest point in the sky.</note>.
**Hypogeion** <note>Original: ὑπόγειον</note>: the bottom of the heaven <note>The point directly beneath the earth.</note>.
**Rising** <note>Original: *Ortus*</note> in Latin: the first part of the horoscope, which in every birth-time first emerges from the eastern part and is led out through the next thirty degrees.
**Setting** <note>Original: *Occasus*</note> is that part of the heaven positioned exactly in the seventh place from the horoscope; in Greek, it is the *diametron dypon* <note>Original: διάμετρον δύπνον. Literally, the setting diameter.</note>.
**Mid-heaven** is the name for the tenth sign from the horoscope.
**Bottom of Heaven** is that which is positioned in the fourth place from the horoscope.
**Thea** <note>Greek: Θεα, meaning 'Goddess.'</note> is the third place from the horoscope, that is, the third sign from the horoscope.
**Theos** <note>Greek: Θεὸς, meaning 'God.'</note> is that sign which is positioned opposite this sign in diameter, that is, the ninth from the horoscope.
**Good Fortune** is the fifth place from the horoscope; in Greek, *agathe tyche* <note>Original: ἀγαθὴ τύχη</note>.
**Agathodaimon** <note>Original: ἀγαθοδαίμων</note>, that is, the **Good Spirit**, is opposite "Fortune" in diameter; that is, in the eleventh place from the horoscope.
**Idle and Dejected places** are what they are called when they are joined to the horoscope by no association <note>In astrology, these are signs that do not "behold" the Ascendant by any major aspect.</note>.
**Anaphora** <note>Original: ἀναφορά</note>, or the **Infernal Gate**, is what the first... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; 'Anaphora' usually refers to the 2nd house or the rising of a star.</note>

# ON THE DEFINITIONS AND TERMS

**The cast-down place** <note>original: *deiector locus*</note> is the location established in the second sign from the horoscope <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the Ascendant or 1st House; the second sign is the 2nd House, which ancient astrologers sometimes viewed as "falling away" from the strength of the horizon.</note>.
**The descent**, or the **upper gate** <note>original: *ἐπικαταφορά* (epikataphora)</note>, is the diameter opposite the aforementioned sign—that is, the eighth place from the horoscope.
**The lowest places** are those of "bad fortune" and "evil spirits."
**Bad fortune** is the sixth place from the horoscope; in Greek, it is called **bad fortune** or **bad spirit** <note>original: *κακὴ τύχη ἢ κακοδαίμων* (kakē tychē ē kakodaimōn)</note>.
**Opposition aspect** <note>original: *aspectus diameter*</note> is the one stretching from a sign to the seventh sign away, such as from **Aries** to **Libra**.
**Trine aspect** is the one from the sign where we begin to the fifth sign, such as from **Aries** to **Leo**.
We call it a **Right trine** when it is behind the sign from which we begin.
A **Left trine** is one that is in front: for instance, the right trine of **Aries** is **Sagittarius**, while the left is **Leo**. In the same way, the right trine of **Leo** is **Aries**, and the left is **Sagittarius**.
**Square aspect** is the one from the sign where we start to the fourth sign, such as **Aries, Cancer, Libra,** and **Capricorn**.
Whichever is behind is called a **Right square**, such as **Aries** and **Capricorn**.
**Sextile aspect** <note>original: *hexagonus*</note> is the one from the sign where we begin to the third sign.
**Giver of life** is the master or lord of the birth chart <note>Known in astrology as the *Hyleg*.</note>.
**Heavenly elements** <note>original: *οὐράνια στοιχεῖα*</note> are the celestial figures or signs.
**Benefics** <note>original: *καλοποιοί* (kalopoioi)</note> are the planets that bring good fortune.
**Malefics** <note>original: *κακοποιοί* (kakopoioi)</note> are those that bring misfortune; they are otherwise called the "evildoers."
**Astrological judgment** <note>original: *ἀποτέλεσμα* (apotelesma)</note> is the decision or sentence of the stars; in Latin, it is a prediction or judgment.
**Secondary signs** are those perceived within the elements of nature themselves, such as comets, earthquakes, rains, and excessive droughts. They are called "secondary" because they possess secondary powers, whereas the primary power resides in the heavens and the celestial stars. The secondary power is in the elements that are stirred up within themselves.
**Corrupting stars** are those that assist the decrees of the celestial stars; they are the phenomena that occur in the elements with excess and a certain greater force, such as droughts and heavy rains. They are called "corrupting" because every excess of the elements brings about corruption.
**Secondary stars** are those that have a secondary and prosperous power implanted in them.
**Cuspids of heaven**, **angles**, **centers** <note>original: *τὰ κέντρα* (ta kentra)</note>, and **pivots** all refer to the same thing <note>These are the four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note>.
**Succedent houses** <note>original: *ἐπαναφοραί* (epanaphorai)</note> are the houses that follow the angles.
**Eclipses** <note>original: *ἐκλείψεις* (ekleipseis)</note> are the failures and darkenings of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>.
**Androdas** is the 63rd year of life; it is so named because, for hidden reasons, it always affects a person with various critical dangers <note>The "Grand Climacteric" year, thought to be especially dangerous because it is 7 x 9 years.</note>.
**Septenary and Novenary years** <note>original: *Hebdomatici & Enneatici*</note> are years in cycles of seven and nine, which always portend heavy evils for men—

<column-break/>

—tending toward danger.
**Full degrees** in a figure are called those in which **decans** are found <note>A decan is a subdivision of a zodiac sign, spanning 10 degrees.</note>.
**Empty degrees** are those which the number of decans never reaches.
**Northern signs** are the names for those that move from the beginning of **Aries** to the end of **Virgo**.
**Southern signs** are those that turn from the beginning of **Libra** to the end of **Pisces**.
**Signs of direct ascension** <note>Also known as signs of long ascension.</note> are named from the beginning of **Cancer** to the end of **Sagittarius**.
**Signs of crooked ascension** <note>Also known as signs of short ascension.</note> are said to ascend from the beginning of **Capricorn** to the end of **Gemini**.
**Agreeing signs** <note>These are signs of equal power or light, often called antiscions.</note> are **Aries** & **Leo**, **Cancer** & **Capricorn**, **Gemini** & **Sagittarius**, **Leo** & **Sagittarius**, **Gemini** & **Libra**.
The **Greatest half** of the circle is called that which stretches from the beginning of **Leo** to the end of **Pisces**.
The **Half of the Sun** is the same as the "greatest half," because the **Sun** has its primary influence in this entire half, just as the planets have in their own boundaries.
The **Least half** is that which is from the beginning of **Aquarius** to the end of **Cancer**; it is called the **Half of the Moon**, because the **Moon** similarly has its primary influence in this entire half, just as the **Sun** does in the greatest.
The **Hot half** is from the beginning of **Aries** to the end of **Virgo**.
**Decuries** are the faces of the signs <note>Another term for decans.</note>.
**Fixed stars** are so named because their motion is barely perceived after a hundred years, which seems the longest span of a human life.
**The Pleiades** <note>original: *Πλειάδες*</note>, in Latin called the **Vergiliae**, are so named because they rise at the end of spring when summer begins. The Babylonians call them **Atarage**.
**The Hyades** were called the **Little Pigs** <note>original: *Suculae*</note> by the ancients; some place them in the mouth, others in the forehead of **Taurus**.
**The Torch-bearer** <note>original: *Λαμπαδίας* (Lampadias)</note> is the brightest among the Hyades and their leader. In Chaldean, it is called **Aldebaran**.
**Anhelar**, the star of Apollo, is the star shining in the head of **Gemini**.
**Abrachaleus**, in Greek "the star of Hercules" <note>original: *ἡρακλέης ἄστρον*</note>, is in the very back of the head of **Gemini**.
**Azabenae** are stars located at the Claws <note>The "Claws of the Scorpion" was an older name for the constellation Libra.</note>, retaining the qualities of **Saturn** and **Jupiter**.
The "Claws" for the Latins are the **horns**, which are imagined much like those in **Cancer** and **Virgo**.
**Nebulous cluster** <note>original: *νεφελοειδὴς συστροφὴ* (nepheloeidēs systrophē)</note> refers to a cloudy mass. The **Nebula** in the breast of **Cancer** is otherwise called the **Manger** <note>the *Praesepe*</note>, and in Chaldean, **Meellephi**.
**The Little King** <note>original: *Βασιλίσκος* (Basiliskos)</note> is the bright star at the heart of the **Lion** <note>Regulus.</note>.
**The Asses** are the stars situated at the Manger itself.
**The Vintager** <note>original: *Vindemitor*</note>, in Greek **the Herald of the Vintage** <note>original: *προτρυγήτωρ* (protrygētōr)</note>, and in Chaldean **Almucediem Alaraph**, is the bright star at the northern wing of **Virgo**.

# OF ASTROLOGY.

**Spica** <note>original: *στάχυς* (stachys); called *Abzumon Alazel* in Chaldaic</note>, located in **Virgo** ♍.
**Antares** <note>original: *ἀντάρης* (antares)</note>, the **Heart of Scorpio**, a notable and bright star located among those three distinct stars on the back of **Scorpio** ♏.
**The Southern One** <note>original: *νότης* (notēs)</note>, that small fish which is to the south, called the **Northern [Fish]** in Latin. <note>The author may be referring to the two fish of the constellation Pisces, which have distinct northern and southern positions.</note>
**The Bond** <note>original: *συνδεσμὸς* (syndesmos)</note>, the series of stars between **Pisces** and **Aries**; the Latins call it the **celestial node**.
**Arcturus** is well known.
**Ophiuchus** <note>original: *ὀφιοῦχος* (ophiouchos)</note>, the **Serpent-Bearer**.
**Life-giving places** <note>original: *ἀφυτικοὶ* (aphytikoi)</note>, or "lawful" places, also called **Hyleg** <note>A term for the planet or point that acts as the "giver of life" in a birth chart</note> as the Chaldeans call them; otherwise known as **Climacteric** points.
**Climacteric years**, or years of progression, are so named because from the risings of the planets—calculated according to the straight or oblique circle of the Climate—the time is known when a planet will reach a certain place.
**Significator of the Kingdom**, a planet that holds more and stronger prerogatives in the midheaven <note>The highest point of the chart, representing career and public life</note>.
**Ruler or host of the interlunium**, the lord of the place where the conjunction of the **Sun** ☉ and **Moon** ☽ occurred.
**Interlunium**, that is, the **new moon**, in Greek called the **synod** <note>original: *σύνοδος* (synodos)</note>.
The **Idiocrator** planet <note>original: *ἰδιοκρατωρ* (idiokratōr)</note>, that is, the ruler who holds dominion over the others.
The **Oikodespotes** planet <note>original: *οἰκοδεσποτης* (oikodespotēs)</note>, that is, the "head of the family" planet; the same is also called the **lord of the birth** and the **master of the nativity** <note>original: *κύριος γενέσεως* (kyrios geneseōs)</note>.
**Kakosis** <note>original: *κάκωσις* (kakōsis)</note>, a bad condition or the affliction of the eleventh house.
The **Schema** <note>original: *σχῆμα* (schēma)</note>, the entire arrangement of the heavens.
**To direct** is to investigate a certain degree of the Equator rising or setting with some arc of the ecliptic, or another current interval, the **Hyleg**, and the harmful star or its ray. For whenever a harmful star or harmful rays meet the Hyleg in this way, they cut short life and portend that danger is imminent.
**Day**, the passage of the **Sun** above the earth.
**Our hemisphere**, that half of the earth described by our horizon.
**Biothanatoi** <note>original: *βιοθάνατοι* (biothanatoi)</note>, those who perish by a violent death.
**Eminence**, elevation, or the sublimity of a planet, occurs in conjunction when the planet itself is carried in the highest part of the upper circle—called an **epicycle** <note>original: *ἐπίκυκλος* (epikyklos)</note> in Greek—while the other planet holds the lower parts. They also call this place by the common name **Apogee** <note>original: *Augem*</note>. Pontanus, a most elegant writer, calls it the **apex** and the **summit**.
**Anairetic places** <note>original: *ἀναιρετικοὶ* (anairetikoi)</note>, lethal places in the figure of the heavens that bring the danger of death.
**The Cutter** <note>original: *πονιστὴρ* (ponistēr)</note>, the planet’s progression to a lethal place, which today is improperly called the **abscission** <note>cutting off</note>; and that planet is the **Abscisor** planet.
The **permeating** or **receding** planet, the **Podistes** planet <note>original: *πόδιστης* (podistēs)</note>, which is itself **sectarian** <note>original: *αἱρετικὸς* (hairetikos)</note>, a **condition-**

<column-break/>

**ary** planet, or one that is of that condition, whether nocturnal or diurnal.
**Hora** <note>original: *ὥρα* (hōra)</note>, the lord of the hour.
**Horokrator** <note>original: *ὡροκράτωρ* (hōrokratōr)</note>, the lord of the bounds <note>specific subdivisions of the signs</note>.
**Under the rays** <note>original: *ὑπαυγὴς* (hypaugēs)</note>, a planet positioned under the rays of the **Sun** ☉, that is, "sub-radiated." Because this word seemed too harsh, it pleased more modern writers to call it **combust**.
**Decans**, or **decuries**, are the same thing. Each ten-degree segment of the signs were called **Faces** by Haly <note>The Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel</note> and Guido <note>Guido Bonatti</note> in their own fashion.
**Paranatellonta** <note>original: *παρανάτελλοντα* (paranatellonta)</note>, the constellations that rise together with the decans.
**Lord of the full moon** or **new moon**, not that planet which rules the sign in which the opposition or conjunction occurs, but rather the lord of the sign that is rising at the time of the conjunction or opposition.
They are called **Trajections**, a new name some today give to "crossing stars," such as **leaping goats**, **torches**, and **fiery beams** <note>Historical terms for meteors, comets, or atmospheric fire</note>.
The **Standard-bearer**, in Greek the **Zodiac** <note>original: *ζωδιακὸς* (zōdiakos)</note>.
They are called **Degrees**, the 30 parts of each sign, divided into equal measures. The ancient Latins also called them **parts**.
**Month**, that whole space of time in which the **Moon** ☽ returns from the **Sun** ☉ back to itself.
**Year**, that space of time until the **Sun** ☉ returns to that place from which it had departed twelve months before.
They are called **Solstitial signs** because when the **Sun** ☉ has traveled to them, it is believed to stand still for a time before its movement to the north or its decline to the south becomes more manifest; these are **Cancer** ♋ and **Capricorn** ♑.
**Almugea** in Chaldaic, the aspects of the planets among themselves.
**Harmful and threatening aspects** are the square and opposite aspects, and the diameters.
**Benevolent aspects** are those from triangles [trines] and hexagons [sextiles].
Stars placed in the **upper hemisphere** are said to "behold" the horoscope <note>the Ascendant</note> with a **right irradiation**, whether it be a sextile, square, or trine.
Those located in the **lower hemisphere** gaze upon each other with a **left radiation**.
**Platic aspect** <note>original: *πλατικὸς* (platikos)</note>, which is by sign only, where the signs themselves behold each other.
**Partile aspect**, when as many degrees of the heaven as constitute the configuration itself exist between star and star. For example, when the first degree of **Aries** rises from the east, and the first degree of **Libra**—in which a harmful planet is positioned—is falling into the lower hemisphere in the west, or in a degree not very far distant.
The **pivot of the rising heaven**, today called the **Ascendant**.
**Epochs** <note>original: *ἐποχαὶ* (epochai)</note>, the degrees at which the planets are found in the Zodiac.
**Moira** <note>original: *μοῖρα* (moira)</note>, the space of a single degree.

### ON DEFINITIONS AND TERMS

**First minutes** <note>original: *πρῶτα λεπτὰ* (prōta lepta)</note>, or primary minutes.
**Second minutes** <note>original: *δεύτέρα λεπτὰ* (deutera lepta)</note>, or secondary minutes <note>These refer to what we now call minutes and seconds of arc or time</note>.
The **meridian circle** is that which the **Sun** ☉ marks when it comes directly over the heads of men, thereby creating the middle of the day <note>Noon</note>.
**Seal-makers** <note>original: *στοιχειωματικοί* (stoicheiōmatikoi)</note>, those who create sigils and images from mixtures of substances according to the courses of the stars, whether to heal diseases or to procure other effects for the body or the soul.
**Mathematicians** <note>original: *μαθηματικοί* (mathēmatikoi)</note> was the name first given to the disciples of Pythagoras, because they professed Geometry, Gnomonics <note>the art of sundial making</note>, Music, and other such disciplines; the ancient Greeks called these "the subjects of learning" <note>original: *μαθήματα* (mathēmata)</note>. However, the common people used the name "Mathematicians" for those who ought to be called by their ethnic name, **Chaldeans** <note>In the Roman era, "Chaldean" was a common term for an astrologer</note>. Later, those who were distinguished by these scientific studies proceeded to the observation of the works of the world and the principles of nature, and only then were they called **Physicists** <note>original: *φυσικοί* (physikoi)</note>. Source: Aulus Gellius.
**Cubes** <note>original: *κύβοι* (kyboi)</note>, four-sided figures.
A **line** is **length without breadth** <note>original: *γραμμὴ μῆκος ἀπλατές* (grammē mēkos aplatēs)</note>.
The **Wagon** <note>original: *ἄμαξα* (amaxa)</note>, a celestial chariot. Our ancestors called it the **Seven Oxen** <note>original: *Septentriones*</note> after the yoked oxen, because the seven stars are shaped like yoked "Triones" <note>plowing oxen</note>.

->**NAMES OF THE WINDS,**<-
->from Gellius.<-

The **Eurus** wind, blowing from the spring east (that is, from the equinoctial point), otherwise called the **Apeliotes** <note>original: *ἀπηλιώτης*</note>; Roman sailors called it the **Subsolanus**.
**Aquilo**, or **Boreas**, which comes from the summer or solstitial rising point; Homer called it the **generator of clear skies** <note>original: *αἰθρηγενέτης* (aithrēgenetēs)</note>. They think it is called **Boreas** from the word for **shouting** <note>original: *ἀπὸ τῆς βοῆς* (apo tēs boēs)</note>, because its blast is violent and loud.
**Vulturnus** blows from the [winter] east; in Greek it is **Euronotus**, because it sits between the South Wind (Notus) and the East Wind (Eurus).
**Caurus**, in Greek **Argestes**, blows opposite to Aquilo.
The other is **Favonius**, in Greek **Zephyrus**; this blows opposite to Eurus. See Strabo on this matter in the first book of his *Geography*.
**Africus**, in Greek **Lips**, blows opposite to Vulturnus.
**Auster**, in Greek **Notus**, is a southern wind, so called because it is cloudy and moist; for in Greek **notis** <note>original: *νοτίς*</note> signifies moisture.
**Septentrionarius**, or in Greek **Aparctias**, is set directly opposite to the South Wind (Auster).
**Circius** is a wind known primarily to the Gauls, blowing from their own land, most fierce and whirling.
**Iapix** blows through the borders of Apulia.
**Fate** is called **Pepromene** <note>original: *πεπρωμένην*</note> and **Heimarmene** <note>original: *εἱμαρμένην*</note> by the Greeks. It is, as Chrysippus says in Gellius, a certain eternal and unalterable series of things, a chain rolling itself upon itself and entangling itself 

<column-break/>

through eternal orders of consequence, from which it is fitted and connected together.
The **Appearance** of a planet is said to occur when a planet, which for some time lay hidden beneath the solar rays, begins to appear in the morning or the evening.
A planet is said to **hide beneath the solar rays** when it is fifteen degrees before or after the **Sun**.
**Hayz**, or the "similitude" of a planet, is when a daytime planet is above the earth by day and below the earth by night; and a nighttime planet is below the earth by day and above the earth by night; and when a masculine planet is found in a masculine sign and quadrant and is oriental <note>rising before the sun</note>, whereas a feminine planet is found in feminine signs and quadrants and is occidental <note>setting after the sun</note>.
**Good configurations** of the planets are considered to be the conjunctions of good planets with other good planets, and good aspects—namely, the **trine** and **sextile** <note>angles of 120 and 60 degrees</note>—of the luminaries <note>Sun and Moon</note> to each other, or with the planets, or of the planets among themselves.
**Bad configurations** are the conjunctions of "malefics" <note>Mars and Saturn</note>, and their aspects of **opposition** and **square** <note>angles of 180 and 90 degrees</note>.
The **greatest debility** of a planet is called **Combustion**.
**Retrocession** <note>appearing to move backward</note> also diminishes its strength significantly.
A planet is called **Combust** when it is distant from the **Sun** by less than half of its "orb" <note>the sphere of its influence</note>, whether precisely that much before or after.
The **half-orb** of **Saturn** ♄ and **Jupiter** ♃ is nine degrees.
The half-orb of **Mars** ♂, **Venus** ♀, and **Mercury** ☿ is seven degrees.
The half-orb of the **Moon** ☽ is twelve degrees.
The half-orb of the **Sun** ☉ is fifteen degrees.
A planet **progresses** when its motion recorded in the **Ephemeris** <note>a table of predicted celestial positions</note> increases.
A planet is said to **retrograde** when its motion decreases.
A **planetary station** is said to occur where the planet is varied by no motion of degrees or minutes.
A planet moves **swiftly** when its true motion is faster than its mean <note>average</note> motion according to the sequence of the signs.
It is said to walk **more slowly** when it is retrograding or proceeding slower than its mean motion.
A planet is called **increased in light** when it moves away from the **Sun**, or the **Sun** moves away from it.
A planet is **diminished in light** when it approaches the **Sun**, or the **Sun** approaches it.
The **argument of latitude** of the **Moon** is the distance of the lunar head <note>the North Node</note> from its own "Dragon's Head" <note>another term for the North Node</note>.
Planets are called **Enemies** when they have opposite houses. For example: **Saturn** and the **Moon**, for **Cancer** ♋ (the house of the **Moon** ☽) is opposite to **Capricorn** ♑ (which is the house of **Saturn** ♄).
There is also **enmity** among planets by reason of their **exaltations** <note>signs where their power is most amplified</note>. In this manner, **Jupiter** ♃ is the enemy of **Mars** ♂, since his exaltation is in **Cancer** ♋, and that of **Mars** ♂ is in **Capricorn** ♑, which...

## ON ASTROLOGY

These are the opposite signs.
Planets agree in nature, quality, substance, and power: **Aries** ♈︎ agrees with the **Sun** ☉ in heat; **Venus** ♀ with the **Moon** ☽ in cold and moisture; **Jupiter** ♃ and **Venus** ♀ in nature.

The **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*</note> is named from "light" <note>original: *lumen*</note>, because she shines through the reflection of the Sun’s light.

The **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*</note> received his name either because he "alone" <note>original: *solus*</note> among the stars is the most powerful, like a prince and leader; or because he has his light from himself and does not borrow it from any other.

**Wandering stars** <note>original: *Vagae* or *vagantes*</note> is the name given to those commonly called **planets** or **strays**.

**Lunar Illuminations** <note>original: *Presulxiones* (likely a corruption of *praeillustraciones*)</note>, which others call the "faces" of the Moon. There are ten in number: **conjunction** <note>original: *coitus*</note>, **birth** <note>original: *genna*</note>, **rising**, **rising into horns**, **divided by the orb** <note>half-moon</note>, **split in two**, which is called <term>dichotomos</term> <note>original: διχότομος; meaning "cut in half"</note>, **full moon**, and again **divided by the orb** and **rising into horns** <note>waning phases</note>. Some add an eleventh, **Plesiphahen**, or as others prefer, **Plesiofelinon** <note>Near-full moon</note>.

The **Conjunction** of the Moon is the name used when she is in the same degree of any sign as the Sun.

The **Birth** <note>original: *Genna*</note> of the Moon is when she has moved fifteen degrees away from the Sun’s conjunction.

The Moon is said to **rise into horns** when, moving away from the Sun, she creates a six-angled figure <note>a sextile aspect of 60 degrees</note>.

The **Divided Moon** is when she has departed ninety degrees from the Sun, making a four-angled figure <note>a square aspect</note> of the world.

The Moon **half-divided by the orb** is when she is 120 degrees distant following the Sun, having a triangle <note>a trine aspect</note>.

The **Plesiofelinos** Moon <note>Near-full</note> is when she is 150 degrees following the Sun—six signs and four parts—but not yet in opposition.

The **Full Moon** <note>original: *Plenilunium*</note> occurs when the Moon is $185.5$ degrees distant following the Sun <note>This value is unusually high; 180 degrees is the standard for opposition</note>.

The Moon is called **Apocrufis** <note>hiding</note> when she has declined one degree from opposition with the Sun.

**Epacts** are the differences between the Solar and Lunar years.

A **Solar Year** has 365 days.
A **Lunar Year** has 354 days.
The difference between these is eleven days, and these are called **Epacts**.

**Beholding signs** <note>original: *Spectantium signa*</note> are those which restore the length of days and nights in equal hours. For the longest hour is fifteen hours when the Sun is in **Cancer**, and the shortest when the Sun is in **Capricorn**.

Signs are said to have **equal power** over each other which have equal rising times <note>original: *anaphoram*</note> and follow one another in turn, such as **Aries** and **Pisces**, or **Virgo** and **Libra**. And if the rising time is equal at three, four, or five signs, such as **Aquarius** and **Gemini**, **Capricorn** and **Cancer**, **Sagittarius** and **Leo**, or **Scorpio** and **Taurus**. These

<column-break/>

some say "hear" each other, but do not "see" each other, because of the shadow of the earth.

**Diurnal stars** are what they call **Jupiter** and **Saturn**; they assert these belong to the faction of the **Sun** himself, because they do not make many settings or figures <note>aspects</note>; for they rejoice to exercise their authority by day, and in the diurnal houses.

**Nocturnal stars** are what they call **Mars** and **Venus**, who are the familiars of the **Moon**. Indeed, they have many figures, and often come to their setting and are obscured.

**Mercury** is a **promiscuous** <note>neutral</note> star: for he becomes the familiar of whichever stars' figures he adapts himself to—morning star to the Sun, evening star to the Moon.

The **Houses of the stars**, **Zones**, or **Girdles** are what they call the twelve "twelfth-parts" <note>original: *duodecatemoria*</note> of the Zodiac, which they also call "signs."

**Apoclimata** are declinations <note>The falling away of a planet from an angle/center</note>.

There are **four Centers**: the **horoscope** <note>Ascendant</note>, the **setting** <note>Descendant</note>, the **midday** <note>Midheaven</note>, and the **place under the earth** <note>Imum Coeli</note> or **hypogium**.

The **Dodecatemorion** is so named because it is the twelfth part of the signs.

The **Figures of the stars** are what they call their testimonies to one another: namely **triangles** <note>trines</note>, **squares** <note>quadratures</note>, **hexagons** <note>sextiles</note>, and **diameters** <note>oppositions</note>.

They call a figure **Right** (triangle, square, or hexagon) when it is the one from which the star has departed; and **Left** when it is the one toward which it goes. For example, with the Sun in **Leo**, the right triangle is **Aries** and **Leo**, but the left is **Sagittarius**. The right square is **Taurus** and **Leo**, the left is **Scorpio**. The right sextile <note>original: ✳</note> is **Gemini** and **Leo**, the left is **Libra**.

Any star spreads **seven rays**: three indeed upwards, and just as many downwards, and furthermore one in diameter <note>opposition</note>. Those to the right are the ones pointing upwards; those to the left are the ones pointing downwards.

They call it **Parallagen** <note>parallax</note> when stars have a change in their isosceles line as shaped by their degrees; such as the Sun in 19 degrees of **Aries** and Saturn in 20 degrees of **Libra**.

**Contact** and **Agglutination** is the name for the meeting and standing together of two stars in one "twelfth-part" <note>sign</note>, at almost the same degree. And **Contact**, which is also named <term>kollēsis</term> <note>original: κόλλησις; meaning "gluing"</note>, can be called "agglutination" in Latin, or "joining" <note>original: *copula*</note>. It happens when they touch in degree, or by body, or in any figure, the preceding star being met by the following one; and if it happens that the one which precedes goes faster than the one following, then one overtakes the other in one degree and touches it, or is not further away than three degrees.

**Efflux** <note>separation</note> occurs when, after contact, the faster star is distinguished from the slower-moving one. Or as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and astrologer</note> prefers, **Efflux** is the name used when a star flows away from another star, the faster from the slower, either from a recently made joining or from a contact through a figure, when more than

# ON THE DEFINITIONS AND TERMS OF ASTROLOGY

[...] join together to form a configuration, they have begun to occupy the middle parts.

A star is called **orbicular** when the following star casts its ray into the preceding configuration.

Signs are called **disjunct** and **averse** which do not form a configuration between themselves.

A star is said to be **circumvallated** <note>original: *circumuallari*; meaning "walled around" or "hemmed in"</note> when it is in such a configuration, specifically enclosed: for example, if the **Moon** is in **Virgo**, and **Mars** is in **Aries**, it encompasses **Virgo**, **Leo**, and **Libra**. One ray of **Mars** is carried into the triangle of **Leo**, while the other goes into **Libra** by diameter; the **Moon** is therefore called circumvallated by the baleful stars.

This is also called an **obsession** <note>original: *obsessio*; a "siege" or "blocking in"</note>, when two stars have in a way enclosed one in the middle, with no other star interposing a ray in between.

It is called a **middle-casting** <note>original: *medius iaculatus*</note> when a star has projected a ray into the middle degrees.

It is called **transvection** <note>original: *transuectio*; a carrying across</note> when a star is joined to another star, and that one in turn to another: for it carries the setting of one into the setting of the other.

It is called an **embrace** <note>original: *complexus*</note> when different and various stars gather around one star: for then that wandering star adopts their power for itself.

It is called **aversion** when the lord of the horoscope <note>In traditional astrology, "horoscopus" refers to the Ascendant, or the point rising on the eastern horizon</note> is not joined to the lord of the signifying horoscope, which pertains to interrogations <note>This refers to horary astrology, where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</note>.

A planet is called **pre-eminent** or **surmounting** when placed in the twelfth sign above one in the fourth: as the one in **Libra** surpasses the one in **Capricorn**, and the one in **Capricorn** surpasses the one in **Aries**.

A planet is called **aphetes** <term>aphetes: from the Greek for "releaser" or "sender forth," a planet that determines the length of life</term> when it moves from the rising to the setting, that is, from the following to the preceding signs.

On the contrary, it is called **prosthetes** <term>prosthetes: an "adder" or "giver of increase"</term>, that is, when it moves from the setting to the rising, namely from the preceding to the following signs.

A planet is called **hypaugos** <note>original: *hypaugus*; from Greek "under the rays"</note> when the **Sun** has overtaken it or hidden it beneath its brilliance and rays.

It is **fluxion** or **emergence** when a planet, fleeing the light of the **Sun**, first flashes forth.

**Morning emergence** is when it first appears at the rising.

**Evening emergence** is when it first emerges at the setting.

There are, furthermore, two places in the sky, distinct from one another by diameter—

<column-break/>

—distinct from one another, which are also called **ecliptic conjunctions**, because the eclipses of the **Sun** and **Moon** occur in them while they are within them. One of their meetings is called **Anabibazon** <note>original: ☋; the ascending node</note>, which more recent authors call the **Tail of the Dragon**; the other is **Catabibazon** <note>original: ☊; the descending node</note>, which they call the **Head of the Dragon** <note>Note that the author has swapped the traditional names; usually the Head is the Ascending Node and the Tail is the Descending Node</note>.

It is called a **confine** <note>original: *confinium*</note> when stars are within the same **terms** <term>terms: specific subdivisions of a zodiac sign ruled by different planets</term>, whether in a completed bonding and union, or a configuration, as when they occasionally behold one another within the terms of the same star.

**Void of course**—called **kenodromia** <note>original: κενοδρομία</note> in Greek—is when the **Moon** is joined to nothing, neither by degree, nor configuration, nor by bonding, and indeed is not going to come into conjunction within nearly 30 degrees.

**Exhalma**, which is also called **exaltation**, is when the **Sun**, **Moon**, or the **Lot of Fortune** <note>a calculated point in a chart representing prosperity</note> from the birth <note>original: *genesis*</note>, exiting a sign in their progress, fall into the following sign.

**Ecptosis**, or **falling away**, is when the year derived from the horoscope <note>the ascendant</note> falls into that sign where the preceding conjunction was at birth.

There are five **releasing places** in the hemisphere above the earth: the **Midheaven**, and two signs on either side (namely the following and preceding signs), the **horoscope**, and the **setting** <note>the descendant</note>.

The **releasers** are four: the **Sun**, the **Moon**, the **Lot of Fortune**, and the prevailing lord of the birth itself.

Stars are said to be placed **in their splendors** when they are positioned in their own house, or their exaltation, or their own terms.

**Participation** is when a companion is of the same sign, or beholds the planet favorably.

The **participant** of a sign is a co-ruler.

**Co-ruling** occurs when the house of one is the exaltation of another.

**Resolution into the opposite**, which is called **anachysis** <note>original: ἀνάχυσις</note>, is when day stars occupy the houses or exaltations of night stars, or night stars those of the day; or when stars placed in signs announce well, but the lords of the signs are troublesome in their malice.

**Malice** is when one is struck by destructive rays, or is besieged, or is in contact with something destructive, or is in conjunction, or comes into opposition, or is surmounted, or is possessed in rulership by a destructive and poorly-disposed planet.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE MATHESIS BY JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS THE 
## YOUNGER, A SICILIAN OF SENATORIAL RANK, TO MAVORTIUS 
### Lollianus.
#### PREFACE.

<image-desc>An ornate square woodcut border enclosing the decorative initial letter 'O'. The interior of the letter contains a scene with a reclining figure in a landscape, possibly representing a shepherd or a mythological figure. The border is decorated with Renaissance style scrollwork and foliate motifs.</image-desc>

**O**nce, Mavortius—our great honor—I promised you that I would publish these books. However, a wavering modesty often held me back and, with a hesitant trembling, called me away from this pursuit of writing; especially since the weakness of my talent could not conceive that it could know anything of such a kind that it would judge worthy of your ears. Indeed, when I remembered that overly bold promise, far beyond my strength, by which I vowed to dedicate to you the entire discipline of divine Astrology <note>original: *Matheseos*; while today this looks like "mathematics," in the Roman era it specifically referred to the "divine science" of astrology</note>, a paleness and a certain rustic fear repeatedly invaded my hesitant mind. 

For when you were established in the high offices <note>original: *fascibus*; referring to the "fasces," the bundles of rods and axes that symbolized the authority of a Roman magistrate</note> of the province of Campania—the administration of which you ennoble with the highest dignity of honor—the rigor of the winter frosts occurred to you. This persuaded you to step away from your affairs and, exhausted by the variety of a long journey of labors, to relax both your mind and limbs for a little while. You most pleasantly turned aside to me first, on these Sicilian shores, seeking especially those studies to which both of us have been bound since our youth. 

There, you strove to relieve the decline of my weak and weary body with the faithful and most sacred comforts of friendship. When health, restored by your consolations and remedies, recalled me to my former state, we shared honorable and varied conversations, together recalling our past deeds and the charms of our younger years. 

But after we talked of our actions and progress, you inquired of me (as you remember) the geography of all Sicily, where I live; you asked after my place of birth and everything the ancients have handed down, seeking an explanation based on true reason. You asked what the true meaning is of Scylla or Charybdis <note>Legendary sea monsters of the Sicilian straits</note>, or the turbulent confusion of the waves rushing into the straits, which separate seas—after a certain time and space—join back together with a contrary collision of waves. 

You asked what the fires do that burst forth from the peak of Mount Etna: what their nature is, what their substance is, and from what origin such great blazes proceed and breathe forth without the destruction of the mountain. You asked about the nature of the lake shown near the bed of the Symaethus river, named Palicus, which is always foul with a pale thickness and turns black with livid foam, and, hissing with a screeching union <note>original: *coniugio*; likely referring to the twin volcanic springs of the Palici</note>, whistles out a sharp murmur. 

Recalling and inquiring with me into all other things which both Greek and Roman literature have handed down to you from your earliest years concerning the wonders of the Sicilian province, you finally transitioned the order of your discourse to the sphere of Archimedes <note>A famous mechanical model of the heavens, or planetarium, attributed to the scientist Archimedes of Syracuse</note>. You showed me the wisdom and learning of your divine talent, asking: What those nine spheres and five zones (colored by different types of nature) might do; what the twelve signs [of the Zodiac] effect; what the eternal wandering of the five stars <note>original: *stellarum*; referring to the five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> brings about; what the daily course and annual return of the Sun means; and the swift motion of the Moon, with the constant increase or loss of its light. 

You asked by what great revolutions that "Great Year" <note>A cosmic cycle where all celestial bodies return to their original positions; Firmicus identifies it here as 1,461 years</note> is completed, which restores these five planets, the Moon, and the Sun to their original places, ending in a circuit of one thousand four hundred and sixty-one years. You asked what logic created the Milky Way; what causes the eclipse of the Sun and Moon; why the rotation of the heavens never moves the "Great Bear" <note>original: *septentriones*; the northern constellations</note> to the west or restores it to the east; which part of the earth lies under the North Wind and which under the South; and what logic suspends the Earth itself, placed in the center, by a balanced moderation of equality. Finally, you asked how the ocean—which they call the Atlantic Sea—encloses the space of the land like an island by the pouring around of its waves. When you had demonstrated all these things to me with easy proof, Mavortius, you ornament of good men...

### THE MATHESIS OF JULIUS FIRMICUS.

...were handed over to their instruction, I even dared to put forward something with the rashness of unadvised speech, promising that I would produce for you whatever the ancient Egyptians—wise and divine men—and the prudent Babylonians have handed down to us through the mastery of divine doctrine regarding the power and authority of the stars. Therefore, as you yourself know, I was reckless in that promise, and—to speak truly with you—I frequently rebuked myself with severe scolding; I desired to change the promise, if it were permitted. But the encouragement of your discourse raised up my trembling and forced me to approach what I had frequently abandoned out of despair. For when the serene and venerable judgments of our Lord and Emperor Constantine Augustus had handed over the governance of the entire East to you, you let no time pass without demanding from us what we had promised you in an unadvised pledge. Therefore, to you as Proconsul and Ordinary Consul-designate, we return our promises: praying and asking for pardon, so that you do not look for weight or the grace of perfect oration in these books; nor should great treatises, or grave and firm opinions, or monuments of doctrine and eloquence be sought by your judgment. In us, there is a slender talent, a subtle speech, and (it must be truly confessed) very modest Astrology <note>original: *Mathesis*; the term refers to the "divine science" of astrology rather than modern mathematics</note>. Although all these things disturbed us with various despairs, we nevertheless undertook the labor of writing, lest—though placed in arduous and most difficult promises—we should fail the judgments of your wisdom, most learned Lollianus.

Therefore, standing in the vestibule of our speech and at the very beginnings of our principles, we ought to do nothing else but respond to those who attempt to undermine the whole power of Astrology <note>original: *Matheseos*</note> with various kinds of orations—those who think that by the authority of their lofty speech, they can break through all this philosophy and divine science with their opinions and disputes. In my judgment, as the facts themselves prove, it is not the weakness or falsehood of the doctrine itself that provokes them, but rather the zeal of those who contradict, resisting with the pugnacious license of argumentation certain and defined matters—things we perceive not only by the mind and reason, but which we behold with the sharpness and judgment of our own eyes. For thus, by their overly hidden and subtle disputes, they attempt to go from the very responses of the mathematicians, as if through some underground tunnel, to undermine this entire science. Yet the more vehemently they fight, and the more they seek every way to persuade, the more vehemently and strongly they fortify the faith in astrology. For its substance would not be true unless they struggled against it with such great force of argument.

Nor is this worthy of wonder, since we know how much dissension there is among them concerning the nature of the gods themselves, and with how many arguments of dispute they attempt to overturn the whole power of divinity. 
<margin>Various opinions concerning the Gods.</margin>
For some say there are no gods; others define that they exist indeed, but care for nothing; others say they both exist and take up the care and management of our affairs. All these are involved in such great variety and dissension that it would be long and irrelevant—especially at this time when we have undertaken another work—to enumerate the opinions of each one. For some assign shapes to them according to their own will, and assign places, even establishing seats, and describe many things about their actions and lives; they pronounce that all things which are made and established are ruled and governed by their will. Others have said they accomplish nothing, care for nothing, and are free from all care of administration; and they all bring forward something plausible to invite the minds of the listeners to an easy credulity. Indeed, the things said concerning the immortality of the soul by that divine Plato and the most sharp and ardent Aristotle demonstrate contrary and repugnant statements among themselves. For concerning good and evil, their opinions are diverse and shifting among each other; I think the explanation of these should be omitted now, for we have not entered into this kind of dispute, nor have we formed our mind and plan to refute or confirm these things. But we have touched upon all these in a brief speech so that the contentious fictions of those who contradict might be revealed to all men, exposing their own zeal. It is pleasing, therefore, to review what is said about Astrology <note>original: *Mathesi*</note>, and it is our care to touch upon everything said by them in a brief speech. For as we are about to explain the substance of Astrology and star-lore, we ought not to linger longer in the works of others.

# BOOK ONE.
## ON ASTROLOGY <note>original: *Mathesis*; in this context, the term refers specifically to the divine science of astrology and the study of celestial influences rather than modern mathematics</note> AGAINST THE ARGUMENTS OF RIVALS.
### Chapter I.

First, therefore, critics raise points concerning the characters and skin colors of men, saying: if the characters and colors of men are assigned by planetary alignments—as if the courses of the stars composed the features of mortal bodies through a kind of painting and craftsmanship—that is, if the Moon <note>original: ☽</note> makes men white, the Sun <note>original: ☉</note> red, and Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> black: why are all people in Ethiopia born black, in Germany white, and in Thrace red? It is as if the Moon and Mars <note>original: ♂</note> do not have their own force and power in Ethiopia, or as if the planet Saturn abandons its power and license to shape bodies in Germany and Thrace.

Regarding character, they add this: if Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> makes men cautious, grave, slow, greedy, and silent; Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note> makes them mature, good, kind, and modest; Mars <note>original: ♂</note> makes them cruel, treacherous, and fierce; the Sun <note>original: ☉</note> makes them religious, noble, and proud; Venus <note>original: ♀</note> makes them lustful, charming, and shining with an honorable splendor of grace; Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> makes them astute, clever, and turbulent with the shifting movements of a stirred mind; and the Moon <note>original: ☽</note> makes them sharp, splendid, elegant, and prevailing through the grace of popular brilliance: why are certain nations formed in such a way that they are recognizable by a certain uniformity of character?

The *Scythians* alone are known for their monstrous and savage cruelty. *Italians* are always distinguished by a royal nobility; *Gauls* are dull; *Greeks* are flighty; *Africans* are deceitful; *Syrians* are greedy; *Sicilians* are sharp; *Asians* are always lustful and occupied with pleasures; and *Spaniards* are distorted by a high-minded boastfulness.

Therefore, does Jupiter never mitigate the madness of the *Scythians*? Or will the Sun never deny empire to the *Italians*? Does the planet Saturn not impose weight upon the flightiness of the *Greeks*? Is *Asian* lust not corrected by the sober moderation of Jupiter? Is the sharpness of the *Sicilians* never dulled by the cold rising of Saturn? Is the greed of the *Syrians* not tempered by the lustful radiations of Venus? Will the healthy star of Jupiter not hinder the malicious schemes and double-tongued <note>The Latin *bilingues* refers to being deceitful or treacherous</note> souls of the *Africans*? Will the sluggish light of Saturn be unable to blunt the boastfulness of the *Spaniards*? Nor will Mercury, the wisest star, sharpen *Gallic* dullness?

Meanwhile, their most powerful and vehement argument against us is their claim that, according to the principles of this art, all the duties of virtue are removed from human affairs. If temperance, fortitude, prudence, and justice are granted by the decrees of the stars and not by our own wills, then we no longer depend on the constant practice of virtue, but solely on the influences of the stars. On the contrary, if someone breaks the bond of society and charity, neglects the laws of human reconciliation, and hands himself over entirely to ferocity and treachery following his own crime and the perverse desires of his mind, he may ascribe it to the judgments of the stars. Let him be unjust, treacherous, malevolent, and irreligious, because a bad constellation of Mercury with Mars performs these vices; he may then attribute the vice not to himself, but to the stars that impel him. 

Why then do we strengthen our minds with the study of fortitude? Why, formed by an upright mind, sublime constancy, and the mastery of divine virtues, do we despise death and pain when placed in bitter circumstances? Why seek the praise of glory and the insignias of the most powerful dignity, if the Sun, in the fellowship of a good conjunction with Jupiter, grants these to us even if we do not seek them? It is in vain, then, that we suppress the vices of an erring mind through counsel and reason; in vain do we temper the lustful allurements of desire; in vain do we seek the modesty of equity and laws through the instinct of gravity—if Venus, tempered by the good radiations of Jupiter and the Moon, inflames us toward the desires and cravings of that virtue.

They even confront individual men with this line of reasoning: "It is in vain, O good man, that you choose good things or desire to flee from evil, if you feel yourself compelled toward them from elsewhere. Why do you fortify yourself with honorable plans and the help of diligence, if all this is provided to you not by knowledge, but by either Saturn or Jupiter?"

Let us therefore (if it seems right) despise the gods and make public the sacred and venerable ceremonies of religions with a sacrilegious heat of despair, if we can achieve all things without their divine power, helped only by the stars. Why do you, O plowman, call upon the gods? Without the care of your divinity, by the influence of the stars alone and the nature of the crop, the furrow is made level. You, who along the open ridges arrange the line of vineyards in distinct rows, in vain do you dedicate the shoots of the vines to your Liber <note>The Roman god of wine and fertility, often identified with Bacchus</note> with religious trepidation, if they are either denied or given by the course of the stars without the protection of divinity. You, who promulgate laws and [rig...] <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page</note>
