IVLII FIRMICI MAT.

...away with sacred things, remove decrees, break the law-tables, and free us from these most severe punishments. Mercury ☿ (as the astrologers claim) made that man a temple-robber; Venus ♀ made that one an adulterer; the star of Mars ♂ armed that one for the slaughter of men. It forces one to forge documents, another to mix poisons; Mercury ☿ forces still another to summon the peaceful souls of the dead with wicked incantations, even those purged by the forgetfulness of the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, Lethe is the river in the Underworld from which souls drink to forget their past lives before reincarnation</note>. Look, that man is inflamed with incestuous passions; you see another clinging to the embraces of boys; we attribute the cause of such great evil to Mars or Venus ♀. And yet that man, by your command <note>Addressing a judge or magistrate</note>, is struck down by the hand of the executioner without cause; the sentence pronounced against him is wrongly spoken if he was forced to sin not by his own desire, but by the defective radiation of the stars. You magistrates have no just basis for punishment, because you know we are always incited to these vices by the malignant fuel of the stars.

They compose these and other similar speeches, asking whether we say the stars are animate or inanimate beings, so that, confused by the conclusion of this question, we might find it difficult to bring forth our mind's judgment and opinion. For whichever of these is said, they turn it to the contrary with the stings of syllogisms <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises; here used to mean clever rhetorical traps</note>, so that the speech of those responding, constrained by their will, might agree with them. In these matters and disputes, we indeed praise their cleverness, but we avoid their purpose and method; because astrology <note>original: *astrologia*</note> has proved its own credibility to us through the divine and most manifest authority of its answers and outcomes <note>original: *apotelesmatum*; technical term for the completed effects or predictions resulting from planetary positions</note>. 

Some even add—in order to agree with us on another point, yet still disturb this entire science with the despair of doubt—that this teaching indeed has the greatest power, but because of the smallness of the parts and minutes <note>Refers to the precise division of the zodiac into degrees and minutes, requiring extreme mathematical precision</note>, the very swift course of the stars, and the steep slide of the heaven’s rotating whirl, no mortal can reach a clear understanding. Thus, by their plausible definition of the matter, the very substance of the whole science is undermined. But we, though our talent is thin and the speech of our narrow oratory almost ineffective, while we ought to refute what they say through the truth of the thing itself, and confirm the precepts of this divine science by the consistency of its answers and outcomes, we shall nonetheless respond. We ask for indulgence from you, Lollianus (our pride), so that in all refutations, the reliability of truth, and not the splendor and substance of oratory, may be sought.

### THE DISSOLUTION OF OBJECTIONS. CHAPTER II.

**A**nd first, I would wish that this vehement accuser of Astrologers <note>original: *Mathematicorum*; in the Roman era, "mathematicians" almost always referred to practitioners of astrology</note>, who pursues this art with such lofty speech, would declare whether he has ever undertaken any experiment of the science itself: whether no one gave him true answers when he inquired, or whether, scorning to listen and fearing his ears would be polluted by such answers, he—stern, vehement, and in a way disturbing the laws of all divinity—has sharpened the stings of his arguments with the license of a practiced speech. 

If true answers were given to him when he asked, and the reliability of truth followed the practitioner's opinion, why does he criticize what he ought to have admired? Why does the treacherous accuser attack the divine science with the mind of a traitor? If, however, because of erratic answers, the one who professed to know Astrology <note>original: *Mathesin*</note> could not fulfill what he said, and his answers stained his promise with lies, only his lack of skill and his rashness should be struck at, not Astrology itself, and it is the deceptive promise that should be shamed. For he is worthy of every evil, because through him the study of so noble an art is overshadowed by the false lies of his answers. 

But he who refused to ask or hear anything, nor provided the judgment of his ears to those who answer truly—fearing, presumably, that the reliability of truth would break his rigid thoughts—acts unjustly if he thinks he should criticize whatever he could or could not perceive with the dulled focus of his mind. For judges who pronounce on things unknown to them are always unjust, as we know. Nor do they have the authority to judge, who are brought to a decision by the ignorant license of rashness. Hence, if he attacks after having heard, believed, and approved something from a most wise Astrologer, he has conceived his notable desires for contradiction from a malicious instinct of mind and a combative zeal. If, however, an unskilled practitioner gave false answers to his inquiry, let not Astrology, but the deceptive and rash ignorance of the man be marked. But he who wished neither to hear nor to judge, in vain claims for himself the [right] of pronouncing...

<meta>This page continues the defense of astrology against skeptics. Firmicus Maternus argues that those who have not practiced the "divine science" are unfit to judge it. He begins to explain the neo-Platonic view of the soul—divine in origin but clouded by its descent into a physical body—and how the study of the stars is actually an act of divine remembrance.</meta>

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>The soul polluted by vices.</margin>
...divides the parts: because he who has not wished to gain experience in a matter is not fit to be able to judge its substance. As for the fact that some people try to deter us from this study by pointing out the difficulty of the science, we gladly embrace it. For these are indeed arduous and difficult things, which a soul—entangled in the snares of earthly filth—cannot easily perceive through simple investigation, even though the soul itself was formed by the fiery immortality of divinity. Its divinity, which is sustained by eternal motion, suffers a temporary loss of its divine nature when it is enclosed in an earthly body; its power and substance are dulled by the union and fellowship with the physical body and the constant threat of the dissolution of its immortality. Thus it happens that all things pertaining to the investigation of the divine arts are always passed down to you through difficult study. Therefore, because we have gladly and easily agreed on this point—showing why divine matters are discerned only through difficult inquiry—it is necessary for the critic to confess that the soul, which is immortal, can easily achieve the investigation of the divine mind if it is separated from the chains and lusts of the earthly body, and if, retaining the constancy of its origin and seed, it recognizes the power of its own majesty. Tell me, who else has seen the path of the sea in heaven? Who, by the rubbing of stones, has struck out the spark of hidden fire? Who has known the powers of herbs? <margin>The power of the soul.</margin> To whom has the whole nature of divinity revealed and betrayed itself, if not to the soul? This soul, having set out from celestial fire, was sent in to rule and govern our earthly fragility. The soul itself handed down the reasoning of this science; it provided the calculations; it showed the courses, retrogradations, stations, fellowships, increases, and the rising and setting of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars—which we call "wanderers" but the Greeks call "planets." <note>original: "planetæ"</note> Even while stationed in the fragility of an earthly body, through a brief recollection of its own majesty, the soul did not "learn" all these things in order to pass them down, but rather "recognized" them. <margin>The star of Saturn ♄.</margin> Behold, the soul recognizes and discovers in which sign the star of Saturn rejoices, and when its coldness grows warm by the fuel of another's heat. Look, we track its motions and courses through individual days and hours. We even predict when it will turn retrograde to its former station; when the neighboring power of the Sun <note>The Sun was often viewed as the "King" or "Heart" of the cosmos, influencing the speed of planets near it</note> might drive its sluggish course with the authority of royal majesty; when the heat of the Sun, departing from it, might grant rest to its slow movement; and after how much time it arrives again with sluggish effort at the same part of the sign from which it had once departed. <margin>Jupiter ♃</margin> These same things are discerned in the star of Jupiter by the same and equal reasoning; for although it runs through the twelve signs in a shorter space of time, it traverses them with a similar motion. <margin>Mars ♂</margin> Even Mars, whom you see as blood-red with the fiery heat of lightning and terrifying with the flash of a threatening light—behold, when it comes to the moist house of Saturn, <note>Likely referring to Capricorn or Aquarius, signs ruled by Saturn, which were associated with cold or water in ancient qualities</note> it tempers its fires with the nature of another's coldness. And although the courses of this star are agitators, it is discerned by that same reasoning. <margin>Venus ♀, Mercury ☿</margin> The daily services of Venus and Mercury have also been shown to us. For these stars, with a short space coming between them, either run ahead of the Sun’s orb together or follow it; or one star, following behind, yields the service of going before to the other. We know when they appear to us at the evening or morning rising, when they hide concealed by the Sun's orb, and when, freed from the splendor of its rays, they shine forth with their own clear brightness. <margin>The Moon ☽</margin> What do you think of the course of the Moon? We have learned when it replenishes the losses of its worn-down orb with its solemn supplements, and when, impoverished of light, it acknowledges the loss of its own majesty. For when it is near the Sun, whether it be waxing or waning, it lowers the rays of its light as if worshipping the Sun; so that, adorned again by its brother’s fires, <note>Ancient astronomers understood that the Moon reflected the Sun's light</note> when it makes the goals of its course longer, it may carry around the ornaments of its light, reborn and renewed with shining splendor. <margin>Eclipse.</margin> Behold, we learn something even greater, which, when it happens, always disturbs unskilled men with a monstrous fear. When the Sun, in the middle of the day, is hindered by the rays of the Moon as if by certain obstacles, it denies the glowing lights of its splendor to all mortals. This event—to speak of recent examples—was predicted to happen for all people by the sagacious intention of the Mathematicians <note>original: "Mathematicorum"; in this context, the term refers to practitioners of the "mathesis" or astrology/astronomy</note> during the consulship of Optatius and Paulinus. <note>This refers to the solar eclipse of July 17, 334 AD, providing a date for the writing of this text</note> And again, when the Moon fails in a similar way, shadowed by the regions of the earth's heights—something we have frequently seen happen in the serenity of a clear night. The genius of the Mathematicians collected all these things and, through skillful calculation, [led to] divine discussion...

<meta>This page continues Julius Firmicus Maternus's defense of astrology (the "Mathesis"). On the previous page, he argued that the difficulty of the science is a result of the soul being weighed down by the physical body. Here, he begins to compare the discovery of planetary paths (astronomy) to the interpretation of their effects (astrology) and addresses the "geographic" argument against astrology—the question of why people of certain regions share physical characteristics like skin color.</meta>

# JULIUS FIRMICUS ON THE MATHEMATICAL ARTS

...has thoroughly learned the secrets of nature. I would wish you, whoever you are, to answer me when I ask: what do you think is more difficult? To find the paths of the stars—which I have now explained—which are carried now through the heights, now through the breadths, now through the depths? These stars join themselves now to the southern regions and winds, now to the northern; now they set, now they are hidden; now moving in a <term>direct course</term><note>The standard forward motion of a planet through the zodiac.</note>, now <term>retrograde</term><note>The appearance of a planet moving backward in the sky due to the earth's relative position.</note>, and now they stand still in <term>stationary</term> slowness, confusing the focus of those searching for them with the sheer variety of their paths. Is that more difficult, or is it harder to define—once the paths are found—what their mixture and radiation accomplishes throughout the entire circuit of the earth?

For you are compelled by the very truth of reason to agree that we found these paths of the stars through constant observation and calculation. Therefore, you must also agree that once the stellar paths were found, we could easily judge their duties and powers. <margin>Every beginning is difficult.</margin> For things are always difficult and arduous when we approach them as the unrefined and unlearned, with the trembling of inconstancy. We cannot easily master by reason anything that preceding teachers have not handed down to us. In this same way, we first learn the shapes of letters with a certain bitter struggle. Or, when set upon an unknown journey, we nearly falter at the very first steps. You see how students first learning <term>arithmetic</term><note>original: "computos"</note> move their fingers with slow, hesitant motions. You see a swimmer falter from the frequent fear of drowning; but a little later, strengthened by the constant movement of his arms, he glides through the highest foam of the waves and supports himself with an easy, light mobility. We run through all these things—letters, math, music, and the other things we learn—with easy logic only when a steady discipline has grasped the way of their first origin. 

Therefore, since it is clear that it was more difficult to find the paths of the stars than to define what they do (for there is no doubt about the paths themselves, which we demonstrate to those wishing to learn first by calculation and then by the vision of the eyes themselves), why do you attack this science? By agreeing with its principles and parts, you strengthen its entire substance.

### THE CONFUSION OF ARGUMENTS. CHAPTER III.

It follows that we should discuss colors and character, and refute this whole area of slanderous questioning with the true strength of arguments. Once all things are discussed and cleared away, we may come safely to the venerable secrets of the science itself. 

The critic says: "Why are all people in Ethiopia black? Why are they fair in Germany? If the courses of the stars, through the diverse mixture of their radiation, bestow shapes and colors upon men?" 

In this part of the inquiry, we ought to fight with a copious speech so that these clever and slanderous fabrications might be conquered by the strength of mature oratory. However, we have restricted our entire effort to the strength of truth alone. We do not want to use the allurements of flowery speech or the license of argumentation to lead the ears of our judges toward the follies of false opinions. 

First, I would like the critic to answer me: in this very population where we are currently living, is there one single, identical form for all men, even though their nature is one and the same? I think he will say that our citizens are all formed with a dissimilar variety of faces, and that the form of all is not one and the same. And if he doubts this (which I do not think he does), let him look when a multitude of the whole people has gathered in one place, as usually happens in theaters or public assemblies. Let him turn the sharpness and judgment of his eyes to the form of the whole crowd and show me, if he can, even two people among so many thousands of men who appear to be formed with the same and identical features of limb and face. 

Let fathers, children, and brothers step forward together. Even though they are joined by the bond of a single blood, they are seen with different designations of form. No one is found so similar to another that his face does not differ in some part from the face of the other. From this it is clear that the substance of our race—the form of the naked and solitary body—is formed from the mixture of the <term>four elements</term><note>Earth, water, air, and fire: the physical building blocks of the universe in ancient science.</note> by the craftsmanship of a provident divinity. <margin>To what extent the power of the stars is distributed among us.</margin> But our colors, forms, characters, and even our institutions are distributed to us from nothing else but the eternal motion of the stars' path. For the stars have their own perception and divine wisdom; for by the pure concept of an animated divinity, they serve that highest and most upright—

# BOOK ONE.

...obey God the Ruler, who arranged all things by the disposition of eternal law to preserve the order of perpetual procreation, with tireless agreement. <margin>On earth there is no holy wisdom.</margin> For there is no man so driven by a sacrilegious despair of rashness as to say that wisdom exists on earth, where he sees all things are mortal, yet would define with an obstinate animosity of mind that in the heavens—where all things are adorned with the perpetuity of immortality—there is no wisdom, no reason, and no order of providence. Who doubts that through these stars, that divine mind is infused into earthly bodies by the necessity of a certain law? To this mind, a descent is granted through the orb of the sun, and an ascent is prepared through the orb of the Moon <note>original: "D", the symbol for the Moon (Luna)</note>. <margin>The divine mind governs all things.</margin> For that divine mind and celestial soul, positioned throughout the entire body of the world in the manner of a circle, and placed now within and now without, governs and arranges all things; and conceived by the generation of its own origin, it perpetuates itself in the procreating and preserving of all things by a fiery and eternal motion. It does not set aside this duty through any fatigue, so that it may sustain itself, the world, and all things within the world by a perpetual and tireless mobility. From this soul, these eternal fires of the stars—which are formed in the likeness of a spherical roundness and complete their circles and orbits with swift haste—animated by the majesty of that divine mind, transfer a part of the soul to earthly bodies and borrow their spirit from those perpetual fuels of the mind. By this reasoning, the immortal soul within us adorns the decaying fragility of the earthly body with the confidence of its own majesty, so that it may respond, in some part, to its own author and origin. This soul, diffused through all living beings born of earthly conception, ensures that, animated by divine fuel, they flourish through the perpetual propagation of generation.

Therefore, since we are now joined to the stars by a certain kinship, we ought not to deprive them of their own powers through sacrilegious disputes, for we are both formed and created by their daily courses. Thus, you are mistaken in your claim that we call men away from the worship of the gods and from religion through a profane madness of mind when we say all our acts are accomplished by the divine courses of the stars. You are wrong, you think the opposite of the truth, and you disagree too much with true reason. For we are the ones who cause the gods to be feared and worshiped; we demonstrate their divinity and majesty when we say that all our acts are governed by their divine motions. Let us therefore worship the gods, whose origin has joined itself to us through the eternal motion of the stars, and let the human race always look up to their majesty with suppliant veneration. Let us humbly invoke the gods and religiously return the vows promised to their divinities, so that our minds, strengthened by divinity, may in some part resist the violent powers of the decrees of the stars. 

The man of divine wisdom, Socrates, taught that we ought to do this. <margin>Socrates.</margin> For when someone had spoken to him about his own character and desires—which that person had gathered through a similar reasoning <note>This likely refers to a physiognomist who claimed Socrates was naturally prone to vice based on his features.</note>—Socrates said: "They are as you say; I acknowledge and confess it." Thus, that wisest of men revealed the hidden vices of his body with an easy confession. "But," he said, "all these things have been overcome by me through wisdom and the authority of virtues; and whatever vice the body held from its base composition, the divinity of the mind, well-conscious of itself, has tempered." From this, it is given to be understood that what we suffer, and what goads us with certain inciting fires, belongs to the stars; but it belongs to the divinity of the mind that we resist. As for the laws by which the sins of men are punished with severe correction, the most prudent antiquity established them rightly. For through these laws, it brought aid to the struggling soul, so that through them, the force of the divine mind might purge the ruinous vices of the body. 

But now, to the one who led us to this necessity of the question, having delayed the response concerning characters and colors—the foundations of which have been laid in part—let us also show that laws serve the power and necessity of the fates, and that they always do what the authority of the fates has decreed. <margin>He indicates the force and necessity of the fates through examples.</margin> To prove this, we must recall longer examples. Behold that young man: healthy in strength, rich, innocent, and modest, driven by no impulse of domestic crime, compelled by no trembling of fear, yet he hung himself with a noose and perished. Another...

<meta>This page continues Julius Firmicus Maternus's argument from Book One of the *Mathesis*. Having established that a divine mind governs the universe through the stars, he now addresses the apparent injustices of life—why the wicked prosper and the good suffer—attributing these reversals not to chance, but to the inescapable power of Fate determined by celestial movements.</meta>

# JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS

While he was already gasping for breath, the enemy <note>Likely referring to death personified or a hostile fate</note> broke the noose; and he who, out of shame for his life, had delivered himself to death by his own hand, is freed from the loosened noose by the sentence of a judge. Who else accomplished this but the power of fate and necessity? Even the ministers of death, who had been appointed to present the accused, ended up liberating a man overwhelmed by his own misfortunes and condemned by the judgment of his own conscience from the very midst of imminent death. On the other hand, another man, to whose innocence everyone bore witness, fell upon a drawn sword as if he were being forced, and buried the threatening point of the blade into his innocent ribs. Consider that man of integrity, sober and modest, whose life and principles we have always admired: behold, his body was cast down a precipice and scattered in a mournful tearing of limbs. Yet another, a just man, sustains his life through wretched begging. Meanwhile, he who is stained by the infamy of a notorious crime is raised up by fortunate increases and burdened with the highest marks of honor. Behold the pirate: after the infinite slaughter of innocents, he receives happy children into his bloodstained lap. But the innocent man, removed from all contagion of crime, is separated from every gift of happiness by the envy of wicked men.

To whom do you attribute these things? Who permits them to happen in such a way? Who has been granted such power over us? Give me your hand, and finally free us from these conflicts of contention, so that you may confirm, even by your own confession, that all these things—which our fragile and decaying mortality is accustomed to bear—are seen to be governed by the chance-like courses of the stars.

<margin>The variety of Fortune.</margin>
What shall we say of the honors given to the wicked, and the flight and exile of the good? Do you see that man, infected with the stains of a slave, protecting the filth and disgrace of his lineage with the nobility of the consular fasces? <note>The *fasces* were bundles of rods and an axe, symbolizing the high authority of a Roman consul.</note> Another, carrying the ornaments of free-born blood, is deprived of the marks of honor due to him. One man, positioned at the first stage of his life and displaying no ornaments of virtue, continues through all honors with headlong speed. Another, now worn out by the old age of a failing life and adorned with the testimony of an excellent life, only now begins his first steps in attaining honors. What old age delayed that man? Or what merit of life promised the other all the ornaments of honor?

<margin>The power of fate is fulfilled by the movement of the stars.</margin>
Who pushed that young man toward such a heap of honors—which we could not have hoped for until now—by a course of sudden happiness, unless that power which we call Fate, which is fulfilled by the movement of the stars, worked to compel him forward while holding the other back?

What shall I say now of the condemnations of the wicked, or of their sins and crimes? You rightly said a little while ago that we have frequently seen injustices of this kind inflicted upon the innocent with the consenting judgment of all.

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
That most prudent Athenian, a man of singular justice who had received the name of "the Wise" by the merit of his life's virtues, was driven out by the cast of a hollow shard. <note>original: "testulæ iactus". This refers to *ostracism*, where citizens voted to exile someone by writing their name on a pottery shard (*ostrakon*).</note> As for Socrates, whose prudence was adorned by the testimony of divinity, who shaped the morals of men and arranged them by divine instruction—he was overwhelmed by false accusations. Burdened by the envy of a bitter betrayal, undefended and betrayed, he succumbed to the severe power of those who judged him.

<margin>Alcibiades.</margin>
How many times did Fortune make Alcibiades a General, and how many times an exile? What shall we say of that variety of fortune? Alcibiades endured these things—though trained in the divine teachings of Socrates for the civil manner of commanding—and although he had led his army successfully always and everywhere, he could not avoid the envy of Fortune raging against him. But perhaps (as some wish to say—though far be it from us to confirm this in our speech) the desires of perverse passions had seized him, and the unforeseen force of reckless daring deceived him.

Do you wish for us to bring forward another example? So that even in this way you may be forced into the constraints of confession?

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Fate sold Plato, despite those virtues of his mind and that doctrine of wisdom; it handed over that discipline of a divine mind to the tyrannical cruelties and mocking powers of Dionysius. <note>Plato was famously sold into slavery in Aegina on the orders of Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note>

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>
If these are not enough, let us return to the shipwrecks of Pythagoras. What kind of man he was is known to all: whose virtue, wisdom, prudence, and the inventions of his divine mind were approved by the judgments of both men and gods. Behold, he lost everything at the peak of his life; and so that nothing might be lacking to his divine genius, having been imbued even with foreign teachings, he penetrated all the secrets of wisdom. And to speak more truly, being first—or rather, the only one—in the intensity of his divine mind, placed within this earthly fragility, he discovered the nature and origin of the provident deity and the divine majesty. For he followed that salutary and provident deity (as some believe) day by day, by whose warnings and...

<meta>This page continues Firmicus Maternus’s discussion of the inescapable nature of Fate. Having previously mentioned the trials of great men, the text here concludes the account of Pythagoras’s exile and death before turning to a lengthy examination of the Neo-Platonist philosopher Plotinus, who, despite his virtue and retreat to Campania, suffered a gruesome end.</meta>

# BOOK ONE

...and by his precepts, having purged the impurities of his soul, he reached all the ornaments of virtue; yet the most severe decrees of his fellow citizens made him an outcast and an exile. <note>Firmicus is concluding the story of Pythagoras, the famous Greek philosopher and mathematician, who lived in exile in Southern Italy.</note> Fleeing his homeland and all of Greece, he first crossed into foreign empires, living as an exile in Sybaris and Croton. But even there, fortune did not detain him for long. For he wandered as a fugitive, now through Locri, now through Tarentum, and through almost all the shores of Italy. Behold, at the last, he is surrounded by raging flames, and along with him a crowd of wretched men is consumed as the fire spreads. What do you say? Do you still disparage fate? And do you despise the power of the stars with stubborn animosity, when you see the bad ends of the good, the prosperous acts of the wicked, and the security of the guilty? To whom do you attribute these things? By whose decrees do you think these things happen? We are unjust if, when all these commands of the fates are decreed for us, we still resist with the animosities of rigid contradiction. In short, it must be answered to you that the present examples exhort us to do this: both he who is guilty is saved by the compulsion of fate, and he who is innocent is condemned, and, forced by fatal necessity, has endured the sentence of severe punishment.

<margin>Plotinus</margin>
Now we come to you, Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism. Firmicus uses his life to argue that even the most "divine" philosopher cannot escape a predestined, painful death.</note>, that singular man, so that we may fortify our allegations with the protection of recent examples. What parts of philosophy did he not touch? Since his doctrine followed the distinctions of his life? Since that which he taught was shown not by the example of another's virtue, but by his own; from whose mouth, as if from some inner sanctuary <note>original: "adyto," referring to the innermost, most sacred part of a temple</note>, divine sentences were brought forth. For that man was composed for all the ornaments of virtue, and formed by every study of divine dispositions: just, brave, provident, temperate; and one who believed he could overcome the impulses of fortune by the reason of providence. First, therefore, he chose for himself a place of quiet residence, so that, separated from all the noise of human conversation, he might free himself from the envy of fortune, intending to devote himself only to the marks of divine instruction, so that against all the threats of fortune, he might arm himself with the whole and incorruptible defense of virtue. Upright with this confidence of mind, he even undertook the care and protection of his body; and so as to leave nothing vacant or naked where the license of raging fortune could exert itself, he established himself in a healthy and pure part of the region.

<margin>Praise of Campania</margin>
For in order to establish his seat, he is said to have chosen the pleasant soil of a city in Campania <note>A fertile region in Southern Italy, famous in antiquity for its mild climate and volcanic springs.</note>: where a quiet moderation of air always sustains all the inhabitants with healthy vigor. Where there is neither the force of winter nor the approach of the burning sun, but a composed temperance is moderated by both; where for men laboring under some sickness, health is restored, nourished by the heat of great springs and the healing warmth of boiling waters. Established there, he first despised the insignia of honors, thinking those to be true honors which the divine mastery of prudence had conferred upon him. No desires for riches had seized him; rather, he thought riches were those things with which the soul, being adorned, could find the author of its own origin. Behold, in a certain part of his discourse (as it seems to me), improvident and incautious, he even attacks the power of fatal necessity; and he chastises with a severe verbal rebuke those men who fear the decrees of fortune, attributing nothing to the power of the stars, reserving nothing for the necessities of the fates, but saying that everything is placed in our own power. It would take too long to enumerate what he felt about individual things, by what reasoning he withdrew them from fatal lot, and how he disturbed this power—that is, of the stars and of fate—with the argumentation of his opinions. But he said these things while still whole and healthy; he never turned his eyes or mind toward the end of Socrates or the death of Plato, certainly (as it is given to suspect) ascribing much to their minds, much to their vices. Behold, while he was secure with that animosity of confidence, the whole power of the fates imposed itself upon him: first his limbs grew cold and stiff with the numbness of his blood, and the sharp vision of his eyes gradually lost the splendor of their fading light. Afterward, through his whole skin, a plague nourished by great humors erupted, so that his decaying body, with limbs failing, wasted away in the death of corrupted blood. Through every day and hour, as the disease crept on, small parts of his internal organs fell away;

<margin>The most wretched death of Plotinus</margin>
and whatever you had seen whole a little while before, the ulceration of his consumed body immediately deformed. Thus with his face corrupted and dissipated, the whole shape of his body departed from him, and in a dead body (so to speak), only the soul remained surviving, so that, consumed by this continuation of heavy disease and forced by his own torments, and by the authority of true reason...

# BOOK ONE

<header>JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS</header>

...overcome by this authority, he felt the force of fate and its power. Shaken by the wasting of his worn-out body, he received the sentence pronounced by fortune. What do you say now about his famous death? Why could virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice—not free him from these punishments of fortune? Thus, he too felt the force of fate and met the end which the fiery judgments of the stars had decreed for him. Worn out by the bitterness of that illness, he taught all men by his own example, not by mere talk, that the force and power of the fates can in no way be despised.

<margin>Miltiades.</margin>
<margin>Themistocles.</margin>
You know again, to return to older examples, what Miltiades <note>Miltiades (c. 550–489 BC) was the Greek general who led the victory at Marathon but died in prison after a failed expedition.</note> suffered after his victory; what Themistocles <note>Themistocles (c. 524–459 BC) was the hero of the Battle of Salamis who was later ostracized and died in exile.</note> endured after his triumphs and his period of rest, entangled in the calamities of hardships—and this by the hands of those to whom they had seemingly restored both liberty and their homeland. Who stirred up the rage of the savage people against them? Who stoked the envy? Who brought about such bitter hatred? So much so that, unmindful of benefits and restored liberty, driven by a heavy instinct of madness and the errors of unrestrained fickleness, they struck down courageous and vigorous men with the bitterness of popular punishment—unless it was the force and necessity of fate, which always rules with tireless power?

<margin>Sulla.</margin>
Let us now return, if it pleases you, to Roman examples. Behold that lazy man, polluted by every infamy and stain—I speak of Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla (138–78 BC), a Roman general and dictator known for his bloody "proscriptions."</note>—who, from the first step of his youth, grew up in the laps of buffoons, selling his modesty for profit. Yet he led the army successfully so many times; and so that he might so often be called "The Fortunate" <note>original: *felix*</note>, he caused the countless shipwrecks of the Roman Republic. Look back at how many times he was stained with civil blood, while the vitals of the fatherland were torn apart.

<margin>He enumerates Sulla's crimes.</margin>
Behold, he posts countless lists of proscriptions <note>Proscriptions were posted lists of names; anyone on the list was stripped of citizenship and could be killed for a reward.</note> and is enriched by the murderous collection of blood-stained money. But now, though it is difficult to list all his crimes, we will list a few so that from them you may recognize the force of fatal necessity. Seven thousand of our citizens fell by Sulla's punishment in the very heart of the city of Rome. Believe me, no other force, no merit of sins, no will of the gods, but the necessity of the fates pushed that multitude into Sulla's hands. What kind of judgment do you think this is? What order of reason? That he—who was never mindful of his own sex, who beyond the charm of his youthful years, as a worn-out old man, persisted in bodily shames in another's age, besieged by vices—should govern the Roman Empire?

<margin>Censorinus.</margin>
Now we knew that in his praetorship <note>A high-ranking Roman judicial and military office.</note> he was cast down from his bid for office, when the very grave man Censorinus charged him with the crime of plundering a province with true and firm accusations. He who, as a legate <note>A high-ranking military officer or deputy.</note> in the Cimbrian War, prostrated by the fear of a degenerate mind, abandoned the General Marius and the Roman army. Yet he, though polluted by such great infamies, was later decorated with the authority of royal majesty and turned our army toward our own destruction.

Allow me to recount the crises of Sulla’s crimes in a longer speech; for all these things will contribute to the merit of my argument, if the necessity of the fates is explained fully and most truly through many kinds of misfortunes.

<margin>Sulpitius.</margin>
By Sulla's order, Sulpitius, the tribune of the plebs <note>An elected official representing the common people.</note>, was struck down by the wicked punishment of a murderous command. Imbued with this crime by his tyrannical and wicked greed, Sulla immediately practiced all kinds of cruelty without hesitation, so that he might satisfy the unbridled desires of his mind every single day with the shedding of civil blood.

<margin>Marius is miserably tortured.</margin>
For the man of praetorian rank, namely the younger Marius <note>The son of the great general Gaius Marius; he was a leader of the faction opposing Sulla.</note>, who by the judgment of all seemed well-deserving of the Republic, by Sulla's order, his eyes were first crushed; then his arms, torn from the frame of his body, fell, severed at the shoulders. Third, his tongue was cut out, leaving his voice in his throat. Finally, with every part of his body mutilated, his eyes—which had been spectators and survivors—were gouged out. In such a cramped body, so many punishments were found by the wicked executioner of the fatherland, and his life was barely yielded to such great wounds, as his spirit was plucked away little by little while his limbs flowed here and there. But perhaps he raged with such ferocity only against men? Behold, in the lists of proscriptions, he even wrote the names of women and matrons, so that he might exert the bloody power of the sword over all of humanity. Nor does he yet have a limit, since he is satisfied neither by bloody greed nor by the infinite slaughter of citizens. That Roman people, having subdued all nations, after traversing and possessing the globe...

# BOOK ONE

Even the furthest shore of the Ocean was forced to serve the wicked command of Sulla's power. But Sulla, having weakened the spirits of all men with fear and a wretched, trembling horror, set up a third proscription list <note>Proscriptions were state-sanctioned hit lists; anyone on the list could be killed for a reward.</note> amidst the groans of all citizens, right between the protections of the Porcian and Sempronian laws. <note>The Porcian and Sempronian laws were traditional Roman statutes designed to protect citizens from summary execution without trial—protections Sulla's lists completely ignored.</note> Not content with this evil, and as if to ensure no stage of life remained free from his crimes, he killed Lucretius while already a private citizen; 
<margin>Lucretius.</margin>
even after laying down his royal power, his mind's destructive cruelty persisted. Do you want me to tell you anything more—since we are lingering on Sulla's times—about the Servilian Lake? 
<margin>Lacus Servilius.</margin>
At that lake, the severed heads of many senators hung as a display of his monstrous crime. Standing among the very cushions of the gods and placed amid sacred ceremonies, Sulla always looked upon the wounds of the Republic with a sense of security and pride. <note>original: "puluinaria" — these were cushioned seats where statues of the gods were placed during festivals to "watch" the proceedings; Firmicus suggests Sulla treated his own crimes as a divine spectacle.</note> What could be more cruel? He inflicted miserable bereavement on children and wives under the title of a "public disaster." Nothing was allowed to piety, faith, courage, or foresight against Sulla. Where are those now who believe our sins, human and divine, can be punished by law? Look at Sulla, feeding on wicked slaughters; look at him stalking about with tyrannical power, and no divine power opposes his desires. What do you feel? What do you judge? Do you refute what we say? Show us the order of things. Where are the laws? Where are the judgments? We are abandoned by human and divine judgment, because Sulla committed all these things we mentioned with impunity. Therefore, his crimes, though feeding on so much slaughter, are not punished by any whips of the avenging goddesses, nor is there anyone to reveal their pain through words and tears. Even the final funeral fire is snatched away from those killed by him—could justice not see this? Do you say that the sins of men are punished day by day by the avenging gods? All these things, as you see, were done with impunity; fortune did what she wanted with them, and whatever the fates had decreed for each individual was fulfilled through Sulla's savage punishment. And so you may know that we have spoken with true reason, a prosperous outcome followed him even after these evils: he was crowned with the marks of a perpetual Dictatorship and laid down his powers by his own choice. The limbs of the torn Republic and blood-stained money were, by his command, bestowed upon the wealth of ignoble men. After these evils, he enjoyed a quiet security; fattened by an abundance of crimes, he was honored by a decree of the most distinguished Senate and the people with the title of "Prosperous and Perpetual Happiness." <note>original: "felicitatis" — Sulla took the surname "Felix" (The Lucky or Fortunate) to claim that his success was proof of divine favor.</note> Where are those now who deny that our actions are governed by the random movements of the stars? That cruel, treacherous man, who we know stalked through every kind of cruelty, achieved all the honors of dignity in security. Marius, however, after his triumph over Jugurtha and the other nations he subdued, after he freed the city of Rome from both foreign and domestic dangers, after his triumphal purples and his embroidered golden palms <note>Refers to the "toga palmata," the ceremonial dress of a victorious general.</note>, was bound by iron chains. Look, the hero hides as an exile in the marshes of Minturnae; look, he is weighed down by the filth of prison. Do you see how he approaches the ruins of destroyed Carthage as a fugitive? Which God had made Marius an exile or Sulla "the Lucky"? General Paulus promised command to the soldier Marius, and the legate Sulla brought back the Roman army; and yet afterward, by the judgment of fortune, the former became an exile and the latter "the Lucky." In this over-long speech, we have lamented the force and necessity of fate—even through the power of the stars—and the cruel deeds of Sulla's domination. 
<margin>Scipio.</margin>
Scipio, after so many triumphs, after the destruction of Carthage and the overthrow of Numantia, after traveling through Greece, Asia, and Bithynia, and surveying Syria, after the irreproachable acts of his Dictatorship, was crushed within his private walls by the plots of his own household. He died in the bitter agony of death, oppressed by the wicked hands of those who strangled him, finished off by a kind of private execution. 
<margin>Regulus.</margin>
What did loyalty profit Regulus? The force of fate, after the wretched infamy of captivity, prostrated him among the hands of his enemies through a wakeful atrocity of cruelty. <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus was a Roman general famously tortured to death by the Carthaginians, who allegedly cut off his eyelids and kept him in a spiked barrel.</note> What other force—for he had certainly been a vigorous man—handed over 
<margin>Crassus.</margin>
Crassus as a captive with his Roman fasces? <note>The "fasces" were bundles of rods and axes representing a Roman magistrate's power.</note> He was certainly a vigorous man, and his virtues, which shone by their own merit, once protected the Roman armies. 
<margin>Pompeius.</margin>
Pompey, after his fifth consulship, after so many and such distinguished triumphs, at the bank of the Nile river—his neck, unvanquished and royal, which the triumphal purple had so often surrounded—was cut by the sword of a half-man in a wicked kind of death. <note>Pompey the Great was murdered in Egypt on the orders of King Ptolemy XIII’s advisors, whom the author dismissively calls "half-men."</note> 
<margin>Cato.</margin>
Who armed the hands of Cato for his own slaughter? Who [armed] the impure and effeminate desires of Antony...

# JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS

<margin>Cicero.</margin>
...[and] with the mournful and wretched weeping of everyone, gave over the venerable blood of Cicero to death. Caesar <note>Julius Caesar, who was famous for his policy of "clemency" (indulgentia) toward his defeated enemies.</note> had freed certain men from all fear through his own indulgence, yet these were the very men he later armed for the destruction of his own safety. You see how Fortune dominates everywhere and always; you see how varied and always changeable are the outcomes of men. The brave man is overcome by the coward; the inferior man strikes down the good. Justice did not benefit the just man; providence often deceived the chaste. In the pursuit of public office, the unchaste and the dissolute were preferred over the modest and the sober. The vigorous lie low, while the wicked are praised; and whatever benefited one man deceived another through reckless imitation. All these things are brought upon us by the courses of the stars; Fortune wears us down with these variations. Therefore, warned and shaped by so many examples and so many reasons, let us prove the law of fatal necessity—not by the license of arguments or a flood of words, but by a probable and upright judgment of the truth.

But now, even those who used to disagree with our assertion are beginning to agree in some part, saying that there is indeed a certain force of Fortune and Fate, which they call <term>ordained Fate</term> <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην" (heimarmene) — a Greek philosophical term referring to the fixed, causal chain of events.</note>. Yet, in the license of their own discourse, they grant certain things to this necessity and deny others; the law and necessity of the Fates are treated as if they both can and cannot do something. 
<margin>They call it ordained Fate.</margin>
For they want the nature of humans and other living creatures to be joined by a certain fellowship: that because we are created and procreated in such a way that, living for a certain time and completing the course of life, we are returned to that divine spirit which sustains us once the fragility of the body is dissolved—they believe we are subjected to both fate and lot to fulfill this end. Thus, one and the same law of fatal decree would bring about a similar end of dissolution for us and all living creatures. 

However, they claim that everything pertaining to the course of life is placed in our own will and power, so that our living is our own doing, while only our dying seems to belong to fate and lot. I do not know what this division of conclusions achieves; I do not know who could be persuaded by what is being said. If someone confesses that there is a Fate, and says that the end of all things is subject to fatal necessities, he prejudices his own arguments by this very confession. He diminishes the power of Fate in smaller matters but increases it in greater ones, conceding much and more significant power by saying our acts are in our own power, while hauling the end of living back to the license of fatal lot. In such an inept argument, he puffs himself up with the license of his reasoning: while he grants Fate the license to take notice and concedes the command of all power, he denies it the lesser thing—namely, the power of governing a human being. 

For if Fate brings us forth into the light when we are procreated, and opens the gates of life for humans coming into earthly dealings; if, as they themselves confess, whatever is required of us by the necessity of death at the completion of life's course belongs to Fate; if the necessity of the fatal law establishes for us both the beginning and the end of living—then what else is there that is not placed in its power? Both the beginnings of life are granted to those being born through Fate, and the day of death and the end of living are determined by its decrees and judgments. 

Look at that one who dies prematurely in his mother's womb with premature haste, before the formation of the body is even complete. Another, though the formation of the body is finished and he is freed from the narrowness of the mother’s womb, is not revived by the breath of the vital spirit. That one, placed in the very first cradles of life, is abandoned by his fleeing soul amid the cries of infancy. That one falls, deceived by the fragility of childhood. Another, now of adolescent age and trained by a complete education for all the acts of life (which you said just a moment ago were placed in our power), is snatched away by the sudden accident of death. Yet another, through the length of his living, lacking almost every sense and pleasure, and weak in his declining age and flawed senility, unwillingly sustains the long and tedious burden of light. Who is it who assigns death to that one who was not born, or to that one on his first birthday, or to that one shortly after, or to that youth, or to that old man? 

Let such a person find something for us to follow, I pray; let him find something that can instruct us and show the reason of truth to us who are struggling. He will have to say "Fate" at every turn, and the necessity of human death, which distributes the time of living by its own disposition of judgment to all living things born in this earthly gathering, so that it denies a longer substance of living to some and grants it generously to others. It is absurd for one who confesses...

# BOOK ONE.
b
<meta>catchword: to the end-</meta>

[the inevi]tability of human death, which distributes the span of living to all animate beings produced by earthly gathering, according to its own disposition of judgment, so that it denies a longer substance of life to some and grants it to others. It is absurd to acknowledge the necessity of fate and then later to disparage fate; and it is quite unjust for a person to avoid in the following parts of an oration what had been strengthened by a preceding profession of confession. What indeed shall we say about the various outcomes of deaths?

<margin>Diverse forms of death.</margin>
One man, by the compulsion of fate, is hung by a noose; another is struck by the sword; another is submerged in the sea and rivers; another, handed over to raging flames and fire, is turned into ash and embers. One is hurled over precipices; another is crushed by the ruin of falling roofs. A pestilential venomous poison has driven out the soul of one man; another is gradually consumed by the slow heat of fevers. One man, burning with a swift conflagration of inflamed veins, seethes with the violence of sudden heat; the mindless rage of wild beasts tears another to pieces. One suffers his end unharmed <note>Likely referring to a peaceful death or one without external injury, such as a stroke or sudden natural death.</note>; the bite of a venomous serpent constricts all the veins of another unto death. From this, the fates describe for us the variety of deaths. These are those decrees of the stars which we brought forth a little while ago. From this come those wretched ends of illustrious men, and the happy ends of the wicked and the guilty. From this, the life of men is pierced through its various course, with Fortune always decreeing it. From this it is established that the beginning and end of life, and even all our acts, studies, desires, and whatever else pertains to the conduct of human reason, are contained within the inevitable sentence of fatal necessity. Therefore, let us yield, being overwhelmed by the faith of truth; and let us confess, having followed the judgments of true reason, that nothing is placed in our power, but everything is in the power of the fates, so that whatever

<margin>All things must be yielded to the fates.</margin>
we either do or suffer, all of this is conferred upon us by the judgment of Fortune.

### A DETAILED RESOLUTION. CHAPTER IV.

Having explained and treated all these things, which have shown by the discussion of true reason the force of fate and the laws of the decreeing stars, let us return to that question which we left in the first part of this oration—namely, concerning the colors and characters of men. Thus, this question having been cleared away in every respect, and being secured and strengthened by the confidence of constancy, we may explain to you everything we promised regarding this study, Lollianus <note>Quintus Flavius Maesius Egnatius Lollianus Mavortius, a high-ranking Roman official to whom this work is dedicated.</note>. To him who asks: Why do the bodies of men in certain regions always come out with a black color? Why, indeed, does it shine elsewhere with a pure brightness of whiteness? To him who seeks these causes, I will respond with a brief speech of discussion, especially since the learned opinions of many wise men are brought forward regarding this part. In the entire sky, which has a round formation—because it encompasses the lands, seas, and all other things that are within it by a surrounding flow of fiery spirit <note>original: "ignei spiritus" — referring to the "ether" or the vital heat that ancients believed filled the cosmos.</note>—

<margin>The Five Zones.</margin>
the substance of those five Zones themselves is not uniform or similar. For some of them are uniform and have no foreign admixture, while others are composed of a mixed temperament in a balanced moderation. Of these, the one in the middle, set on fire by the lights of the flashing sun and scorched by the burning of eternal heat, is stained with an ignited color of perpetual redness. Truly, two of them, which contain the extreme parts of the world, clinging to the right and left sides, are marked with a blue color and are always flooded with dark clouds; they are besieged by thick ice, eternal frosts, and snows hardened by cold. Between these two cold ones and that fiery one which is drawn through the middle part of the world, the two remaining zones are established, which a mixed temperament of cold and heat

<margin>Temperate Zones.</margin>
has formed with merciful moderation. These are the two Zones that generate every kind of living creature within the borders of the earth from that tranquil moderation of mixing. Through these, the oblique order of the signs <note>The Zodiac, which appears to move at an angle relative to the celestial equator.</note> turns for the rising and setting of all things that are born through all ages. In this [order], the sun and moon, and also the five wandering stars—which are called "planets" by the Greeks <note>original: "planetae à Graecis uocantur"</note>—run their courses with a certain and defined motion, so that according to the course of these stars, every kind of living creature succeeds itself in a perpetual propagation of its kind. The force and nature of these five Zones generates the men of certain nations with a uniform color; yet, even within that face of unity, the bodies of men are varied by whatever radiation of the stars. Therefore, whatever nation of men lies adjacent to that Zone which is scorched by eternal fires, even if

<margin>Frigid Zones.</margin>
it is situated under the parts of that Zone which is formed with composed moderation...

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of astrology and fate. Having previously discussed how the stars determine the manner of a person's death, Firmicus Maternus now shifts to explaining how the stars—in conjunction with geographic location—dictate physical appearance, individual identity, and national character. He concludes this section with a panegyric to the Emperor Constantine and an invocation of the celestial bodies.</meta>

# JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS

...yet for the purpose of shaping the complexions of men, [the sun] borrows fire from its neighboring associations, so that it stains men with a dark hue in imitation of things that have been scorched. Truly, those parts which lie adjacent to the icy zones—which are devoid 
<margin>The Cold Zones.</margin>
and deserted of the sun’s heat and are oppressed by perpetual frosts and snow—cause those nations of men, which the neighboring zone produces, to be adorned with a luster of splendid whiteness. But both in these regions that produce white men, and in those again that produce black ones, the power of the stars works most effectively to vary the forms of men: and for each individual, even if the substance of their color is uniform, the stars assign a different appearance of shape. For how else would individuals recognize themselves by their own bodily features? How would they know their sons, brothers, and relatives? How would they distinguish citizens, foreigners, neighbors, friends, and guests, if the power of the stars did not assign various and diverse faces to each? Let us therefore consider the preservation of the human race, and upon reflection, we shall find what wicked and impious crimes could have been committed there if a single face for everyone had confused those peoples through a total likeness of form. A brother, deceived by the likeness, might enter to his sister as if he were her husband; another might, through the ignorance of such a resemblance, take a wife who belonged by right to another; some might struggle in the conflict of an uncertain dispute over a son; others would not recognize those who had served them only a little while before. Another, born of noble birth, might be dragged away as a slave due to a confused likeness and the error of a stubborn captor, were it not for the fact that a great diversity of faces varied that uniform similarity of color—all of which are tempered by the arranged mixtures and calculations of the stars. Look how the whiteness of one person is sullied in some part by a thin shadow of black color; the black face of another is illuminated by the brilliance of a moderate whiteness. What shall I say now of the hair of the head, into which varied colors secretly creep? What of the sharpness of the eyes, which are always colored with different lights? Behold the bodies themselves, even among those nations and all others, are now tall, now small; 
<margin>The power of the Zones and the stars.</margin>
now slender with a thin frailty, now broader with a heavy thickness. From this, it is proven by clear reasoning that while it belongs to the Zones that men are black or white, it belongs to the stars that, within that variety of color, they are embodied with the variations of dissimilar forms. 
<margin>Various customs of men.</margin>
Regarding the customs of nations, the dispute is superfluous, for we see many Asians—indeed almost all—displaying the marks of sobriety; and the light-headedness of the Greeks frequently takes on the weight of modest gravity; and the unbridled rage of the Scythians is sometimes mitigated by the mercy of humanity; and in the borders of the Gauls, the people grow strong in the wisdom of prudence; and the cunning minds of the Africans are decorated with the ornaments of honest faith; and the vices of boastfulness are cast aside by many Spaniards; and a sudden generosity has changed the greed of the Syrians; nor is it difficult to find fools among those sharp Sicilians; and from the Italians, the commands of empire have frequently been transferred. 
<margin>The Lord Constantine.</margin>
Nor shall we bring forth examples of this matter from afar or from ancient books. Our Lord and Augustus, and Emperor of the whole world—the pious, fortunate, and provident prince, namely Constantine the Great <note>Constantine I, the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity. Firmicus is writing during his reign.</note>, son of the Divine Constantine <note>Actually the son of Constantius Chlorus; "Divine Constantine" here refers to his deified father, though the names are often conflated in manuscripts.</note>, a prince of August and venerable memory—who was chosen by the favor of propitious majesty to liberate the world from tyrannical excesses and to suppress domestic evils, so that through him, the squalor of slavery being wiped away, the gifts of secure liberty might be restored to us; and so that we might set down the yokes of captivity from our already weary and oppressed necks. He, who always fights for our liberty, has never been deceived by the most uncertain fortune of war amidst human chances. Born at Tarsus <note>Historical sources generally place Constantine’s birth in Naissus (modern Serbia), but Firmicus likely uses Tarsus to align the Emperor's birth with specific astrological significance.</note>, holding the rudders of empire from the first stage of his life, he sustains the Roman world with the healthful moderation of governance for the increase of perennial happiness, having obtained these things under prosperous auspices. 

<margin>☉</margin> Therefore, O Sun, best and greatest, who possesses the middle part of the heaven, the mind of the world, and its tempering force, leader and prince of all, who perpetuates the fires of the other stars by the moderation of your flame-bearing light: 

<margin>☽</margin> And you, Moon, who are placed in the lowest regions of heaven, always uncertain with your monthly lights for the continuity of female offspring, you shine by the august radiation of the sun: 

<margin>E</margin> And you, Saturn <note>In the margin, 'E' likely refers to the first of the outer planets in this sequence.</note>, who are established at the very summit of the heaven, you move forward in a sluggish course and with slow motions by the radiation of your star: 

<margin>F</margin> And you, Jupiter <note>In the margin, 'F' refers to the next planet in the descending order.</note>, [protector] of the Tarpeian Rock...

BOOK TWO.

<margin>Mars</margin>
<margin>The Sun</margin>
<margin>Mercury & Venus</margin>
...inhabitant, you who gladden the world and the lands with your ever-healthful and benign majesty, you hold the leadership of the second sphere <note>The author is addressing the Sun, which in the geocentric model of the time was often placed in the "second" or "middle" rank of the heavens.</note>: and you, O Gradivus <note>original: "Gradiue"; an epithet for Mars as the god of war.</note>, ever to be dreaded for your glowing terror, who are contained in the third regions of the sky: and you also, faithful companions, Mercury and Venus: by the consensus of your moderation and the submissive judgment of the Supreme God—who decrees eternal empires for them—grant that the great prince Constantine and his most invincible children, our lords and Caesars, may rule even our descendants, and the descendants of our descendants, through an infinite continuation of ages; so that, with all bitterness of evils driven away, the human race may enjoy the gifts of peaceful happiness. For us, breathe a subtle substance of talent into our minds, so that supported by your protection, we may easily fulfill those things we promised to Lollianus, and explain whatever we have conceived from the divine mastery of the sages through true definitions of thought. But to turn myself to you, Lollianus, I ask that you examine everything said here with the rigid authority of judgment. For every birth (as you know), if it is "soft," will yield fruit, even if premature; but soon, in the span of adult time, it will yield fruit that is more mellow.

# THE SECOND BOOK OF JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS THE YOUNGER, OF SICILY, A MAN OF SENATORIAL RANK, TO MAVORTIUS
## Lollianus.
### PREFACE.

<margin>Julius Caesar.</margin>
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
<margin>The Antiscia of Hipparchus.</margin>
<margin>Nauigius.</margin>
As we are about to write these books on Astrology <term>Mathesis; the Greek term for learning, specifically used by Firmicus to mean the sacred science of astrology.</term>, we must first instruct those who wish to learn these same things, so that, formed by correct beginnings, they may more easily attain the knowledge of making prognostications. For no one can attain true knowledge of it unless he has been educated in the first principles. For our predecessor Fronto, following the *antiscia* <note>original: "antiscia"; points in the zodiac that are mirrored across the solstice axis (Cancer/Capricorn). Firmicus views these as crucial for hidden influences.</note> of Hipparchus, set forth the meanings of the outcomes <note>original: "apotelesmatum"; the astrological predictions or results of planetary positions.</note> as if he were speaking with those already perfect and skilled, prescribing nothing regarding the instruction or the teaching itself. Scarcely any of the Latins have written books of instruction on this art, except for Julius Caesar, who wrote a few verses—and even those were borrowed from another’s work. Marcus Tullius [Cicero], the leader and glory of Roman eloquence, so as not to leave anything unattempted that his divine genius might not reach, himself also responded with a few things about instruction in heroic verses. For this reason, we have translated all those things which the Egyptians and Babylonians said about this art into a teachable style of discourse, so that those who are being trained to explain the fates of men, having been gradually imbued with it, may attain the full knowledge of divinity. But because we have made mention of the ancients, we must not pass over this point with concealment. Fronto followed the *antiscia* of Hipparchus, which have no power and no substance; and while there are indeed true opinions of prognostications and outcomes in Fronto, the study of those *antiscia* is ineffective. He followed them because he had not attained the true reasoning. For those *antiscia* are true—as our friend Nauigius also proves—which the later Ptolemy showed through a true inquiry of definition. We shall show what kind they are in the later parts of this book, demonstrating which part sends rays to which other part. For Fronto wrote the outcomes most truly, which are contained most abundantly in the books and monuments of the Greeks. Therefore, having set aside this dispute for the time being, let us return to the beginnings of our instruction.

<margin>The Sun. The Zodiac.</margin>
The Zodiac, the circle in which the twelve signs are fixed, through which the planets (and also the Sun and Moon) direct their courses, is always twisted by an oblique motion. The twelve signs themselves are called by these names: Aries ♈, Taurus ♉, Gemini ♊, Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, Virgo ♍, Libra ♎, Scorpio ♏, Sagittarius ♐, Capricorn ♑, Aquarius ♒, Pisces ♓. Of these signs, there are diverse kinds. For some are...

### THE HOUSES OF THE STARS, THEIR NAMES, AND THEIR POWERS IN THE SIGNS. Chapter II.

<margin>Various names for the planets.</margin>
<margin>The houses of the planets.</margin>
Out of these twelve signs, the Sun (☉) and the Moon (☽) have each been allotted a single sign. However, the other five planets—that is, Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), Mars (♂), Venus (♀), and Mercury (☿)—each have two signs in which they hold command and have established their <term>domicile</term> <note>A "domicile" or house is the zodiac sign where a specific planet is said to have its primary influence and "residence."</note>. But the Egyptians do not name these stars by the same names that we or the Greeks do. For the one we call Saturn is called *Phaenon* <note>original: "$\phi\alpha\acute{\iota}\nu\omega\nu$"; meaning "The Shining One."</note> by the Egyptians; the one we call Jupiter, the Egyptians call *Phaethon* <note>original: "$\phi\alpha\acute{\epsilon}\theta\text{o}\nu\tau\alpha$"; meaning "The Radiant One."</note>; the one we call Mars is called *Pyroeis* <note>original: "$\pi\upsilon\rho\acute{o}\epsilon\iota\text{s}$"; meaning "The Fiery One."</note> by them; the one we call Venus is called *Phosphoros* <note>original: "$\phi\omega\sigma\phi\acute{o}\rho\text{o}\text{s}$"; meaning "The Light-Bringer."</note>; and the one we call Mercury, they call *Stilbon* <note>original: "$\sigma\tau\acute{\iota}\lambda\beta\text{o}\nu\tau\alpha$"; meaning "The Gleaming One."</note>.

Thus, Leo (♌) belongs to the Sun, and in this sign it holds its house and power; the Moon’s house is Cancer (♋). You see how fittingly and how subtly it is arranged: the Sun is the master of a masculine sign, while the Moon is the master of a feminine sign, so that each sex might claim a house similar to itself according to the quality of its own gender. The other five planets, as we said above, have two signs in which they exercise the power of their command. Yet, of those two signs which each possesses, one is masculine and the other is feminine. So that this may be understood more clearly, let us explain everything specifically. 

Saturn (♄) has his house in Aquarius (♒) and Capricorn (♑), of which Aquarius is masculine and Capricorn is feminine. Jupiter (♃) has his house in Sagittarius (♐) and Pisces (♓), but of these, Sagittarius is masculine and Pisces is feminine. Mars (♂) has established his house in Aries (♈) and Scorpio (♏), of which Aries is masculine and Scorpio is feminine. The houses of Venus (♀) are Taurus (♉) and Libra (♎), of which Libra is a masculine sign and Taurus is feminine. Mercury (☿) has his house in Gemini (♊) and Virgo (♍). Of these, Gemini is a masculine sign and Virgo is feminine.

### THE EXALTATION AND DEJECTION OF THE STARS, AND THEIR CONDITION. Chapter III.

<margin>The exaltation of the stars.</margin>
<margin>The dejection of the stars.</margin>
We must also know what the <term>exaltations</term> <note>original: "altitudines"; refers to "exaltation," the specific degree or sign where a planet's influence is most potent.</note> of the individual stars are, in which they are raised up by a certain natural loftiness of greatness; and what their <term>dejections</term> <note>original: "deiectiones"; also known as "falls," where a planet's influence is weakened or suppressed.</note> are, in which they are placed such that they are diminished, with the power of their authority oppressed. When stars are positioned in their exaltations, they decree signs of the greatest happiness, especially when, in the <term>birth charts</term> <note>original: "genituris"; the astrological chart of a person's birth.</note> of men, the majority of the stars possess the signs of their own exaltations. On the other hand, men are overwhelmed by the misfortunes of ill-luck whenever the greatest part of the stars are positioned in those areas where, through lowly dejection, they lose much of their power. These are called "exaltations" because when the stars are in that part where they are exalted—provided they are in favorable places of the birth chart—they make men blessed. Their dejections, however, make men wretched, poor, ignoble, and destitute, and those upon whom...

# BOOK SECOND.

<note>Signature: b 3</note>

...and upon whom misfortune descends through continuous successions. For this reason, the Babylonians wished those signs in which the stars are <term>exalted</term> <note>An "exaltation" (Latin: *exaltatio*) is a specific sign and degree where a planet is thought to have its most potent or "ennobled" influence.</note> to be their domiciles. However, we, being trained in this tradition, ought to know that all stars decree more effectively in their heights [exaltations] than in their domiciles.

The **Sun (☉)**, therefore, is exalted in the 19th degree of **Aries (♈)**, but is cast down in the 19th degree of **Libra (♎)**.
The **Moon (☽)** is exalted in the 3rd degree of **Taurus (♉)**, and is cast down in the 3rd degree of **Scorpio (♏)**.
**Saturn (♄)** is exalted in the 20th degree of **Libra (♎)**, and is cast down again in the 19th degree of **Aries (♈)**.
**Jupiter (♃)** is exalted in the 15th degree of **Cancer (♋)**, but is cast down in the 15th degree of **Capricorn (♑)**.
**Mars (♂)** is exalted in the 28th degree of **Capricorn (♑)**, but is cast down in the 28th degree of **Cancer (♋)**.
**Venus (♀)** is exalted in the 27th degree of **Pisces (♓)**, but is cast down in the 27th degree of **Virgo (♍)**.
**Mercury (☿)** is exalted in the 15th degree of **Virgo (♍)**, but is cast down in the 15th degree of **Pisces (♓)**.

For this reason, since the individual planets are exalted through these signs, the Babylonians also wished for these to be their houses, saying indeed that the domicile of **Saturn (♄)** is in **Aquarius (♒)**, **Jupiter (♃)** in **Sagittarius (♐)**, **Mars (♂)** in **Aries (♈)**, the **Sun (☉)** in **Leo (♌)**, the **Moon (☽)** in **Cancer (♋)**, **Venus (♀)** in **Taurus (♉)**, and **Mercury (☿)** in **Virgo (♍)** and **Gemini (♊)**.

### THE DECANS OF THE SIGNS AND THEIR
### lords. Chapter IV.

Individual signs are divided into three parts: each part has its own **decan**, so that there are three <term>decans</term> <note>Derived from the Greek word for "ten," a decan is a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign. There are 36 decans in total across the zodiac.</note> in each sign; each of these possesses ten degrees out of the thirty, and they exercise their lordship and power over those ten parts. They possess infinite power and freedom, and they designate the fates of men by the power of their authority. Moreover, the decans themselves are assigned to specific stars: and when a star is within its own decan, even if it is in someone else’s domicile, it is to be regarded as if it were established in its own house. For when placed in its own decan, it performs the same effects as it decrees when established in its own sign. Thus,

<margin>The Helpers.</margin>
Certain authors, however, wishing to explain this topic more precisely, assigned three divinities to each individual decan, whom they wished to be called **Helpers** <note>original: *munifices*</note>, which is <gloss>collaborators</gloss> <note>original: *synergos*</note>, so that throughout each sign, nine Helpers can be found, with individual decans presiding over three Helpers each. Again, these nine Helpers, who they say are established in each sign, divide their powers among infinite divinities: for they say that sudden accidents, pains, sicknesses, chills, and fevers are decreed by them.

JULIUS FIRMICUS MATERNUS

And whatever that may be, which is accustomed to happen to those who are neither hoping for it nor aware of it. ### DIVISION OF THE SIGNS into thirty parts. Chapter V.

Individual signs have thirty parts <note>Latin: *partes*. In an astrological context, these are "degrees."</note>. Moreover, a "part" in a sign is as much space as the orb of the Sun (☉) or Moon (☽) encompasses in its circuit <note>This is a traditional description of a degree, roughly corresponding to the apparent diameter of the Sun or Moon in the sky.</note>; but one part is divided into sixty minutes, and so on from there.
