The second reason is this: there are very many people who, in order to make a great profit, take the <term>prognostication</term> <note>original: "pronosticationem," the art of foretelling future events</note> of another doctrine and attribute it to this science. Many have been deceived by them and were driven to the opinion that, by the power of this science, they could predict many things, thus exceeding the natural limits of its capacity in their judgments. For this reason, their work gave cause for many to despise not only what cannot be known from this science, but even that which is knowable. This reason, like the first, is inappropriate; for <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophia," used here in the broad sense of organized knowledge or natural science</note> is not to be despised because of the ignorance of fools. It is also clear that even good and accurate investigators of the sciences are sometimes deceived—not for the aforementioned reasons, but because of the nature of the thing itself and their own human weakness, since they cannot grasp the full reality required for this science. It also happens generally that we do not arrive at a knowledge of the quality of this matter with absolute certainty, but rather through probability; this is especially true for that which is gathered from many and dissimilar things. It also happens, in addition to this, that the configurations of the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>original: "erraticarum stellarum," referring to the planets</note> were recorded in ancient times; it is through those ancient records that we consider the configurations of our own times which resemble them. Based on their effects, we judge what the men of ancient authority—those observers of things—discovered through the configurations of their own times. These ancient patterns may perhaps resemble our own configurations much or very little, owing to the long duration of their revolutions. Moreover, that these configurations should be exactly like them—so that the things in the heavens and on the earth return to exactly what they were then—is by no means possible. Nor can this be claimed by anyone, unless they were to foolishly and mockingly confess to knowing perfectly that which could never be perfectly known by anyone, or unless they claimed to have reached a point of knowledge for which no mortal life is long enough. For these reasons, we are at certain times mistaken in our prognostic judgments, because the models through which we learn do not perfectly match those by which we judge. For when we examine the occurrences of the air in the atmosphere, they are difficult for us to find because the discovery of the circumstances that exist in the air is burdensome, even if we have discovered the causes through the celestial bodies. And when we speak about the <term>nativities</term> <note>original: "natiuitatibus," the study of the birth charts of individuals</note> of men, we perceive many and significant circumstances in the collection of forces, which by their own nature compel things to vary. For differences in seeds and the qualities of changes assist much; because while any region—and the air of that same region—may be of one and the same type, a single difference in seeds possesses the power to form an image suitable to its species, such as the seed of a man, a horse, or other beasts. Likewise, the places of birth change things with a great variation. For even when the seeds are of one species, such as the seeds of men, and the atmospheric qualities remain the same, the individuals born will obtain many and great differences in body and soul according to the differences of the regions in which they are born. <insert>Foods</insert> <note>The Latin "Tibi" is likely a transcription error for "Cibi" (foods), as evidenced by the conclusion of the paragraph.</note> also and their diverse customs will assist in their future individual alterations. But since not all things agree with the conditions found in the air—even though the power of the air is great—there is a significant opportunity for great help if those who prognosticate solely through the motions of the heavenly bodies are not assisted by these other factors. Those who investigate only through the stars seek what they cannot know perfectly, and are sometimes found to be deceiving. Since this is the case, this science should not be entirely despised and destroyed just because we are sometimes mistaken in it; just as the <term>skill of sailors</term> <note>original: "nautarum solertia"</note>, who frequently err while navigating, is neither despised nor rejected by us. Instead, we ought to remain more attentive and diligent in it. For they promise us difficult and inestimable things; let us not doubt even that which is possible to attend to through it. Likewise, it is not fitting that we investigate all things through it, but only that we investigate by careful inquiry. We also say it is necessary that we grasp their subject matter, and not interpose that which is not suitable. For just as we do not blame <term>doctors</term> <note>original: "medicos"</note> when they seek the causes of illnesses and the qualities of the sick, so it should not be troublesome for us to investigate the materials, the regions, the foods, and all the accidents that have passed.

### CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY’S QUADRIPARTITUM. THE UTILITY OF THE WORK. Chapter III.

How the <term>prognostications</term> <note>original: "pronosticationes," the art of foretelling future events based on the stars</note> of the stars are perceived, and how only those occurrences which happen to the sphere of the air surrounding the earth, and those which occur to men by reason of these, are made known; and how these human occurrences relate to the body and the soul, to their strengths, and to the works which men perform from their first years even to their last; and which things happen from the outside, which naturally and inevitably adhere to the things mentioned before—like a certain bond of love that exists between the body and its substance, and also its companion <note>the soul</note>: and how the connection between the soul, its progeny, and its authority, however much it may happen to them in the remaining hours, has been generally proven. Now, however, we shall indicate the remainder of what was promised, which is to briefly investigate the utility of this work.

But we have proposed first to explain the manner and the intention of knowing the quantities of this science and its fruits. For we say that if we wish to consider the magnitude of this utility as it pertains to the soul, we will find that there is nothing from which the eagerness of the soul receives so great an improvement. Generally, we say that there is nothing in which the soul profits so much as in the prognostications of this science. For through it, we arrive at a knowledge of divine and human things. Likewise, there is utility for the body, since we cannot arrive at those things which are suitable for each person’s <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexioni," the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental temperament</note> except through the knowledge of this work. 

As for wealth and honors, and similar things, we can say what we consider in all of <term>philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophia," meaning the broader study of natural laws and ethics</note>. For philosophy is not in itself intended to lead anyone to the gain of the aforementioned things; yet it is not right that it should be blamed by men. In the same way, this science is not to be blamed for this reason, nor should its great utilities be set aside. Generally, to those who observe the arguments of those who blame this science and say it is of no utility, it will be clear that they have not spoken truthfully. 

For their foolish deliberation was inclined toward this: they said that prognostications of things that occur inevitably are superfluous and useless. To this, their words are flimsy, lacking subtle insight and proper knowledge. For first, we ought to know that things occurring by necessity, when they happen somewhere, will perhaps do much harm unless they are anticipated; and so much so that they may take away sense and memory, or bring so much joy or sadness that the same result follows. But prognostication applies the soul and draws it toward frequent memories of things still far off, so that it holds them as if they were constant and present, and it prepares the soul plainly and gently for the reception of whatever future thing may come. 

Again, it is not to be thought that superior things <note>the movements of the stars</note> proceed toward their significations inevitably, like those things which happen by divine disposition and which are by no means to be avoided, or those which occur truly and of necessity. Rather, we should know that the powers of the celestial bodies occur by divine disposition, which cannot be prevented from truly happening; and likewise that the variation of terrestrial things proceeds by a natural path, which things are varied and accidentally receive the first impulses of superior things. 

Furthermore, some accidents happen to men by a general harm, not from the property of any specific thing—as in a great change of the air, from which we can scarcely protect ourselves, the deaths of many men occur through the excess of the air, or by plague or drowning. These things occur because a great and strong cause always overcomes a brief and weak cause; and because some accidents happen according to the natural and proper complexions of each individual, through any change contrary to them. Since these things are so, it has been proven in general and individual matters that those accidents whose first cause is stronger and greater than all other causes will necessarily happen regardless of opposing factors. 

It should also be known that those things which are not so fixed, when they receive an equally strong opposing force, will easily change; but those which do not find such opposition will follow their primary natures. This happens through laziness and foolishness, not through necessary forces. We see this same thing happen in all things whose beginnings are natural, such as in the natures of certain stones and plants, and even in wounds...

and of abscesses and infirmities, which necessarily produce some effect, some of which are destined to happen unless they are contradicted by something contrary. Similarly, it is appropriate for all those engaged in this science to consider the accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to non-essential qualities or events that happen to a person, rather than random mishaps.</note> that befall men, to provide a natural <term>prognostication</term> <note>original: "pronosticari," to foretell future events based on astronomical signs</note> regarding them, and to ensure they do not adhere to false opinions. In those matters where alteration is possible, we ought to attend to the modes of judgment, as I shall subjoin. When an <term>astrologer</term> <note>original: "astrologus," a scholar of the stars</note> speaks regarding anyone’s <term>nativity</term> <note>original: "natiuitate," the astrological chart of one's birth</note>, saying that when their <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexio," the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within a person</note> is of such a kind, and the change of the air is thus, and the tempered complexion has been altered, then a certain infirmity will follow according to the increase or decrease [of those qualities]. And similarly, if someone who knows the natures of metallic things says that a magnet attracts iron, each of these things will necessarily happen according to the powers of its own nature, unless it is hindered by the ignorance of the craftsman or if a contrary is not applied to it. And the ulcers will not increase nor putrefy when medicine is brought to meet them.

<margin>The nature of the magnet.</margin>
Nor likewise will the loadstone <note>original: "lapis magnetis"</note> attract iron if it is smeared with other substances <note>Ancient and medieval writers often believed that substances like garlic or oil could strip a magnet of its power.</note>. These things which are predicted are not prohibited except by those things which are naturally contrary to them, as has already been indicated. Similarly, it will also happen in those matters concerning men: those who are ignorant of the accidents will suffer them; but when they are known, and if nothing is placed in opposition to them, the primary order of nature will necessarily follow. But if they are foreknown, and someone who knows how to heal them is found, then either they will not happen at all via the natural path previously indicated, or if they do happen, they will occur only in a small measure.

<margin>General prognostications.</margin>
And since the same power exists in general matters as in individuals, it is a wonder why it is conceded by men that a prognostication of general things can be had, and that they can be guarded against. For there are very many who concede the prognostications of the seasons of the year and the clouds of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: "stellarum fixarum," the stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to each other, unlike the "wandering stars" or planets</note> and their configurations, and they occupy themselves much with these. Indeed, they guard themselves against those things which are to come through them, reserving cold things in the summer and warm things in the winter. Generally, they also strive to balance their complexions with tempered mixtures. Likewise, when they wish to guard themselves against misfortunes and accidents that happen at sea, they attend to the clouds of the fixed stars. In the conception of beasts and the planting of plants, they observe the phases of the Moon, which are formed according to the quantity of its light. And what can I say? We have seen no one who ever denied this, or who said it could neither be useful nor exist.

<margin>Of individuals.</margin>
Yet there are some who judge that no one can arrive at prognostications for individuals regarding their own complexion, such as in the increase or decrease of heat or cold, and similarly in the proper complexion of each thing. They also think there are many things against which no one can guard himself. But if it is clear that when we cool our bodies before the arrival of general heat, less heat burdens us, we can do the same in individual matters which increase heat—namely, that we may turn them away from intemperance. This is only because the cause of this deception is the difficult prognostication of individual things, and because very few have it in use; so much so that it is almost the reason why other things are by no means believed. For things having the powers of contrariety are not easily found without those things through whose powers we predict; therefore, for the most part, they are not found perfectly. Wherefore, since the primary natures are always winning out when there is no prohibitor, people have thought that they do whatever happens inevitably, and in such a way that it cannot be prohibited. And as it seems to me, they have thought the same regarding the prognostication itself. But although it might happen that in the greater part the prognostication fails, it would nevertheless be appropriate that we investigate it subtly, because some truth is in it—just as in the science that demonstrates how to preserve health, although it is not the cause of health for all men, yet since it is for some (even if it be a few), it is nevertheless to be sought and loved, and we ought to consider this to be of great benefit. It is also clear that the Egyptians showed the powers of this work to be very great, since in all their medical books, they joined the science of the stars with prognostications, because they knew these things would be of this sort. Nor would they join those things together in the same hour to perform incantations and medicines, to wipe out present or future impediments, whether general or particular, through...

the accidents <note>In this context, "accidents" refers to external influences or physical changes that happen to a person.</note> surrounding the body, unless people have thought that what would come from there neither changes nor turns aside. For this reason, those things of this nature—and the things that follow them—have the power of being contradicted, and were placed in a second order, according to their virtue and potential. They joined the utility of this work with the power of prognosis in the books called "The Demonstrators of Medicine," specifically so that they might grasp the qualities of existing <term>complexions</term> <note>original: "complexionū," the unique physical and mental constitution of an individual based on the four humors.</note> through the stars, as well as the accidents that are to happen through the <term>surrounding body</term> <note>original: "corpus circūdans," likely referring to the atmosphere or the ambient environment that "surrounds" the person.</note>, and their causes. This was so they might be strong in the knowledge of these things, and in the teaching of the care of curable things for the most part; for it is not at all possible that all bodies and their infirmities should be of the same quality of <term>intemperance</term> <note>original: "intemperie," an imbalance of the humors.</note>. Thus, through medicine and through things appropriate or inappropriate for each individual body, they might be stronger in guarding against future infirmities, and might heal those that have already occurred with a remedy in which there is neither imperfection nor deception; and that from this they might reach the highest perfection anyone can attain. This, therefore, had to be stated in a general way. Consequently, we shall now proceed in an introductory manner. We will first reveal those works by which the alterations of celestial things properly happen. We shall follow this according to the natural order established by the experiments of the ancients, and from these, we will first treat the works of the wandering stars and the luminaries, God willing.

### ON THE POWERS OF THE LUMINARIES AND THE WANDERING STARS. Chapter 4.
<note>The "luminaries" are the Sun and Moon; "wandering stars" refers to the five known planets of the time.</note>

It is clear indeed that the work of the Sun's substance is to heat and, in a small way, to dry. The perception of this work is itself more suitable than all other works, and its knowledge is easier, because of the Sun's great size and the manifest change of the seasons of the year. For the closer the Sun approaches the zenith above our heads, the more it heats.

<margin>On the power of the Moon.</margin>
The greater power of the Moon, however, is to moisten. For it is closer to the Earth, from which moist vapor ascends from the bottom all the way to it. For this reason, it changes bodies in this manifest way. For many parts of those things that exist within the body, it matures and causes to decay. It also possesses, along with the Sun, a small amount of dryness in its heat, because it receives its light from it.

<margin>On the power of Saturn.</margin>
The star of Saturn, according to the greater part of its work, cools, and with its greatest cold, it dries slightly. This seems to happen because of its great distance from the heat of the Sun and from the moist vapors that are near the Earth. The knowledge of the powers of this star and the other stars proceeds from the observations of their <term>aspects</term> <note>original: "figurarum," referring to the geometric relationships between planets.</note> as they are compared with the Sun and Moon. For in the orders of changes, which differ according to increase and decrease, we see that some of them vary the qualities of the air in one way, and some in another.

<margin>On the power of Jupiter.</margin>
The work of the strength of the star Jupiter is of a temperate complexion. For the place of its motion is halfway between the coldness of Saturn and the fervor of Mars. For this reason, it simultaneously heats and moistens. And since its nature is more to heat, and it is carried above the other <term>spheres</term> <note>original: "coelos," referring to the celestial spheres.</note>, it is the author of the winds that cause things to grow.

<margin>On the power of Mars.</margin>
The star of Mars properly dries, and the power of its nature burns. For its heat is likened to the heat of fire, and it holds a place next to the Sun, whose sphere is almost beneath it.

<margin>On the power of Venus.</margin>
The star of Venus also, because of the temperateness of its complexion, entirely imitates Jupiter in its works, except that in her the order of Jupiter is reversed. For she heats slightly because she is near the Sun, and she moistens as much as the Moon because of the great quantity of her light; therefore she attracts to herself the vapors that ascend from the humors surrounding the Earth.

<margin>On the power of Mercury.</margin>
The work of the star of Mercury is for the most part to dry, and equally to moisten. For in certain hours it dries humors, because it is never too far removed from the heat of the Sun. In others, however, it moistens, because its place is above the lunar sphere, which is closer to the Earth; and in both of these, its alteration is swift. It also exists as the author of winds, because its motion around the Sun is known to be rapid.

<summary>Ptolemy describes how the planets and luminaries exert physical influence on the Earth through the primary qualities of heat, moisture, cold, and dryness. He argues that understanding these powers allows physicians and astrologers to better predict and treat imbalances in the human body.</summary>

### ON FORTUNES AND MISFORTUNES. Chapter V.

Since the aforementioned figures are as we have described, and they consist of four natures—namely two, heat and moisture, which are creative and active (for nothing receives growth except through them), and two, coldness and dryness, which are destructive (for through them things diminish and cease to be)—the men of ancient authority declared that two of the wandering stars, specifically Jupiter and Venus, and also the Moon, are "fortunes" <note>In traditional astrology, "fortunes" or "benefics" are planets considered helpful or lucky.</note>. This is because their <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and elemental makeup of a body.</note> is temperate, and they possess much heat and moisture. They testified that the works of Saturn and Mars are naturally contrary to the effects of the aforementioned stars, because one acts through intense cold and the other through intense dryness. They added that the Sun and Mercury have dryness in their nature because they provide that effect, and according to the movement of the other stars † with which they have <term>ictisal</term> <note>original: "ictisal," a term derived from Arabic meaning the "application" or "joining" of planets through their aspects or positions.</note>, they compel things to change more than any other stars.

<margin>† Alternatively: the East Wind. <br/> † Alternatively: the West Wind.</margin>
### ON MASCULINE AND FEMININE SIGNS. Chapter VI.

Furthermore, since there are two primary kinds of nature, masculine and feminine, and since the specifically feminine power arises from a moist substance (because this quality is generally found in females, while the remaining qualities are always found in males), it was elegantly said by the ancients that the Moon and Venus, in which there is much moisture, are feminine; but the Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are masculine. They said that Mercury, because it works equally with dryness and moisture, shares in both genders. They also say that the planets, so to speak, "masculinize" and "feminize" according to the shapes they form in their relationship with the Sun. For when they precede the Sun and are <term>oriental</term> <note>Rising in the east before the sun.</note>, they are masculine; but when they follow the Sun and are <term>occidental</term> <note>Setting in the west after the sun.</note>, they are called feminine. The same is proven by the shapes they form on the horizon. For when they are in places from the east to the mid-heaven, or from the west to the point opposite the mid-heaven <note>The lowest point of the sky, or "Imum Coeli."</note>, they are masculine under the earth, because being oriental, they linger in the part from which the wind called † Affabe <note>A transliteration of the Arabic "al-Saba," meaning the East Wind.</note> proceeds. In the two remaining quarters they are feminine, because they occupy that part from which † Adabor <note>A transliteration of the Arabic "al-Dabur," meaning the West Wind.</note> proceeds.

### ON DIURNAL AND NOCTURNAL PLANETS. Chapter VII.

Furthermore, because there are two spaces from which time is made—one of which is day, which is properly masculine because of its heat and its effective, moving power; and the other is night, which is feminine because of its moisture and rest—they said the Moon and Venus are nocturnal, but the Sun and Jupiter are diurnal. They made Mercury a companion to both, as we said before, reporting it to be diurnal in the east and nocturnal in the west. Regarding the two fortunes <note>benefics</note>, they divided them into two modes, though they did this not naturally, but through contrast. For when similar things are mixed with things whose constitution is suitable, their health is improved. But when dissimilar things are mixed with destructive things, their harm is lessened. For this reason, they likened Saturn (which cools) to the heat of the day, and Mars (because it dries) to the moisture of the night. Thus, because of this, each of these will be tempered by the contrast, and their constitution will be likened to the quality of a temperate state.

### ON THE VIRTUES OF THE FIGURES FORMED
### according to the Sun's position. Chapter VIII.

Likewise, the Moon and the three wandering stars positioned above the Sun <note>The "superior planets": Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> take on decrease and increase in their own powers—namely, the figures they form in relation to the Sun. For the Moon, from its first <term>crescent</term> <note>original: "corniculatione," literally "horning."</note> until its first <term>dichotomy</term> <note>The half-moon phase.</note>, moistens; from there until the full moon, it heats; from there until the second dichotomy, it dries; and then until it is hidden and stands directly with the Sun, it cools. Truly the morning stars, from when they appear from under the Sun's rays until their first <term>station</term> <note>The point where a planet appears to stop before moving backward (retrograde).</note>, moisten more; and from their first station until their evening rising, they heat more; from there until the second station, they dry more; and from that point until they are hidden, they cool more. It is clear that when these are mixed with one another, they produce different qualities in the air...

### ON THE NATURES OF THE FIXED STARS. Chapter IX.

<margin>Aries</margin>Since the treatise on the natures of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>Stars that appear to stay in a permanent position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note>, which they take on according to the property of their own works, follows what was said before, let us begin these in order, and let us record their variations as discovered through experience. From these, we shall indicate their similarities with the wandering stars. And first indeed, let us set forth the memory of those which are in the figures of the signs of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>The "circle of signs" mentioned in the text.</note> itself. Therefore, the stars existing in the head of Aries are likened to the combined powers of Saturn and Mars. But the powers of those in its mouth are said to be similar to the powers of Mercury, and also slightly resemble the powers of Saturn. The work of those in its hind foot do not differ from the works of Mars; and those located in its tail follow the powers of Venus.

<margin>Taurus</margin>The <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical and elemental makeup or "temperament" of a star.</note> of the stars in Taurus that sit upon its shoulder is not distant from the complexion of Venus, and also slightly resembles the complexion of Saturn. But for the stars in the top of the head of Taurus, the one which bears a likeness of bright redness and is called Aldebaran <note>original: "Aldebaran," the brightest star in the constellation Taurus, known as the "Eye of the Bull."</note>, its complexion is not far removed from the complexion of Mars. Those positioned at the top of its feet, and in that part from which they draw out the hem of the robe, are equal to the powers of Mercury and Mars. # CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY’S QUADRIPARTITUM <note>The "Four Books" on the influence of the stars.</note> #

<margin>The Fish.</margin>
<margin>The Hare.</margin>

The stars of the Triangle <note>The constellation Triangulum.</note> are well-regarded. Indeed, the stars of the Triangle are not considered to have anything other than the <term>complexions</term> <note>The "complexion" or temperament refers to the specific mixture of planetary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that a star radiates.</note> of Mercury. Likewise, concerning the stars that are arranged in the figures south of the zodiac circle: it is manifest that the bright star formed in the mouth of the Southern Fish <note>Piscis Austrinus; the star is Fomalhaut.</note> is similar to the powers of Venus and Mercury, while those located in the body of the same fish are likened to Saturn in their effects. Moreover, the powers of the stars in the figure of the Strongest One <note>Orion.</note>—specifically those in both of its shoulders—do not differ from the powers of Mars and Mercury. The effects of all its other bright stars do not depart from the effects of Jupiter and Saturn. Also, the last of the stars of the River <note>Eridanus; the star is Achernar.</note>, which is the brightest, imitates Jupiter, while the others imitate Saturn. Those which designate the figure of the Hare <note>Lepus.</note> are not inconsistent with the powers of Mercury and Saturn. Furthermore, all the stars situated in the Dog <note>Canis Major.</note>, except for the one placed in its mouth, also work the same way and are likened to Venus. But the bright star formed in its very mouth, which is called the "twin ascehere" <note>original: "ascehere gemina"; a Latinization of the Arabic "Al-Shi'ra," referring to Sirius.</note>, does not fall behind the works of Jupiter and is slightly associated with the works of Mars. The complexion of the bright star situated in the First Dog <note>Canis Minor; the star is Procyon.</note> is equal to Mercurial complexions and also slightly to Martial ones. The effects of the stars that represent the form of the Great-Hearted One <note>original: "magnanimi"; likely referring here to the constellation Leo, though it is placed among the southern stars in this sequence.</note>, and their bright stars, are likened to the works of Saturn and Venus; but those situated in the heel do not reject Venusian complexions and imitate Mercurial ones, though only slightly. In the constitution of the Raven <note>Corvus.</note>, the polished stars are similar to Saturn and Mars. The bright stars expressing the image of the Ship <note>Argo Navis.</note> are made equal to Saturn and Jupiter. In the Centaur, those which occupy its human form bear a resemblance to Venus and Mars. But the clear stars situated in its equine figure work just as Jupiter and Venus do. Also, the bright stars placed in the form of the Wolf <note>Lupus.</note> are not denied to have Saturnine powers, nor even Martial ones, though only slightly. Those situated in the Censer <note>Ara.</note> are similar to Venus and somewhat to Mercury. And of the complexion of the bright stars in the Southern Crown <note>Corona Australis.</note>, which is called the southern attendant, they do not forget the Saturnine and Martial complexion.

### ON THE STRENGTHS OF THE FOUR SEASONS. Chapter X. ###

The qualities of the strengths of the stars within themselves, as was discovered by the ancients, are these. They say there are four seasons of the year: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. In the time of spring, moisture is stronger. For when the cold of winter has passed, heat begins, leading to the distemperance of the humors <note>The "humors" are the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were thought to be influenced by the seasons.</note> which were congealed because of the winter cold. But in the summer time, because of the approach of the sun to the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point directly above the observer's head.</note> of our heads, heat prevails. In the autumnal time indeed, dryness wins out; for the heat of the past summer has dried up the moisture. In the winter time, because of the removal of the sun from the place of the zenith of our heads, cold overcomes. For this reason, since the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac.</note> lacks a natural beginning, just like every circle, they established its beginning at the sign of the vernal equinox, which is Aries. They took their start from that point because from there the moist complexion grows; just as in living beings, the first part of the years of life is the time in which their complexion exists as more moist, and they established the other seasons in the same order. For in the complexion of all living beings, moisture prevails in the first years, just as in spring; for in those years, life is soft and tender. In the second years, however, up to the perfect standing-still of heat, just as in summer, heat wins out. In the third years, in which one is near his decline and around the beginning of diminishing, dryness is stronger, just as in autumn. And in the final years, in which one reaches destruction, in that time cold overcomes, just as in winter.

In the part which is called the East, dryness is stronger, because when the sun marches through that part, it does not stop drying up whatever the night has moistened; and because the winds which emit their blasts from that part, and are generally called "Orientals," are deprived of all moisture and are drying. The southern part, however, is the hottest, because the sun's heat is great when it lingers in the middle of heaven. And because...

# BOOK ONE.

<margin>West.</margin>
<margin>North.</margin>
This part—which, in relation to our region’s position, is on the right—is generally called the southern part, and the winds that proceed from it are called southern <note>original: "meridiani"</note>, which are hot and parching. The western part, however, is moist, because when the sun stays in that direction, those things which the day has dried out soon begin to become moist; the winds that proceed from there, which we generally call western, soften and moisten. But the northern part is the coldest, for the reasons of heat that weigh upon us are much further removed from us because of the sun's position in the middle of the sky <note>The "midheaven" or meridian.</note> relative to our location. Since it is placed in opposition to the sun occupying the middle of the sky, the winds proceeding from this part are extremely cold and constricting. Therefore, knowledge of these matters is useful and beneficial for recognizing the <term>complexions</term> <note>The specific mixture of the four primary qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> of all parts in every region. This is because it is plain and obvious that the effective power of the stars changes according to the qualities of the seasons, the years, and the <term>angles</term> <note>The cardinal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Lower Midheaven.</note>. For when all things are assimilated to them, their qualities will be pure and without the mixture of any other thing. On account of this, their works will be stronger. For example: stars that are naturally heating are stronger in hot modes; and stars that are naturally moistening are stronger in moist modes. However, their powers are not pure in the presence of the opposites of these modes, but when mixed with other things, they are weak—just as it happens with the powers of heating stars in cold modes, and with the strengths of moistening stars in drying modes. We should not doubt that the same thing happens in all other modes according to the mixture of qualities.

### ON THE FIXED, TROPICAL, AND 
### COMMON SIGNS. Chapter XII.

<margin>Tropical signs.</margin>
<margin>Equinoctial signs.</margin>
<margin>Common signs.</margin>
With these things having been established, it follows that we should add the specific changes of the parts of the circle of signs <note>The Zodiac.</note> as they have come down to us. These are the general seasonal <term>complexions</term> which are assimilated through them. We will also mention some of their properties which are assimilated to the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars in the following sections, after first establishing the powers of the signs in themselves without any other mixture, which we assign to them only by comparing one to another. Indeed, the first distinction of the signs is that some of them are called tropical, some equinoctial, some fixed, and some common. There are two tropical signs: namely, the 30 degrees which follow the point of the summer solstice without interval, which are the degrees of Cancer; and the other 30 degrees arranged to follow the point of the winter solstice, which are the degrees of Capricorn. These are designated by these names for the reason that what occurs in them is manifest. For when the sun reaches the beginnings of these two signs, it then turns <note>The word "tropical" comes from the Greek *tropos*, meaning "a turn."</note> its motion back toward a latitude contrary to the motion it previously held. And when it is in Cancer, it makes summer; but in Capricorn, it makes winter. There are also two equinoctial signs: namely, the sign following the point of the vernal equinox in the nearest place, which are the degrees of Aries; and the sign following the point of the autumnal equinox in order, which is the sign of Libra. These obtain their name from the fact that it happens in them without doubt: for when the sun enters their beginnings, the days are made equal to the nights everywhere. Of the remaining eight signs, which are located between the tropical and equinoctial signs, four are called fixed and four are called common. The fixed signs are those which follow the two solstitial and two equinoctial signs: which are Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius. This is because the changes of the four seasons, which follow the sun's entry into the solstitial and equinoctial signs, take their beginning there; and whether the air is changed to moisture, heat, cold, or dryness, these qualities are "fixed" and appear more clearly whenever the sun stays in these fixed signs. The quality of the air then exists naturally pure, for on account of the long durability of these qualities, it receives their powers most openly. The common signs <note>Now more commonly known as "mutable" signs.</note> are those which appear immediately after the fixed signs, which are Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. They are so called because they are located between the mobile and fixed signs, and with their beginnings and endings, they are assimilated to a nearly natural transition; they share in each of the two qualities—namely, the qualities of the mobile and the fixed.

CLAUDIUS PTOLEMY

## THE DIVISION OF THE SIGNS INTO MASCULINE AND FEMININE. Chapter 13.

They have judged six signs to be of a masculine and diurnal <note>original: "diurnæ," meaning relating to the day.</note> nature, and the six remaining they have assigned to a feminine and nocturnal nature. They arranged them one after another because day is joined to night and always exists alongside it, and because the masculine sexes are near the feminine ones and are frequently joined with them. They took the starting point of this arrangement from Aries for the reasons mentioned before <note>Aries is the start of the zodiac because it marks the spring equinox.</note>; and since males are dominant and active, and it is more fitting that they be preceding and held in higher honor than the passive ones, they began with a masculine sign for this reason. The signs of Aries and also of Libra are masculine and diurnal because the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> stretches over them; from this, the first and strongest motion—which is called the "motion of the firmament" <note>original: "firmamenti motus," referring to the daily rotation of the heavens.</note>—takes its origin. The order of the signs following these two is as we have said: a feminine sign after a masculine, and a masculine after a feminine.

However, some have begun the order of the signs' genders from the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth or an event.</note>, naming one masculine and the next feminine. They began from the Ascendant just as some placed the beginnings of the <term>movable signs</term> <note>original: "signorum mobilium," also called cardinal signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn.</note> at the sign of the Moon [Cancer], because she receives variation faster than any of the other stars. In a similar way, they began the sequence of the genders of the signs from the Ascendant because it exists closest to the East, and they followed the subsequent order as previously described. Some even divided all the signs into four parts, saying that the signs called "morning" <note>original: "matutinalia"</note> and masculine are those positioned from the Ascendant to the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "cœli medium," the highest point of the sun's path.</note>, as well as those opposite to them, from the West to the "angle of the earth" <note>The IC or Lower Midheaven, the point directly opposite the Midheaven.</note>. They called the two remaining quarters feminine and "evening" <note>original: "uespertinales"</note>. They also gave the signs many other nicknames based on the figures [shapes] found within them: for instance, some are called "four-footed," some "wild," and some "of many children" [fruitful], and similar things. But since the reason for these names is obvious, and since these figures can be named in the appropriate place where they will contribute to our knowledge and use, we have decided to remain silent on them here.

The first affinity <note>relationship or connection</note> between the parts of the zodiac circle that are similar to one another is that found in their figures [aspects]. These are like the parts between which there is the length of one diameter—which are subtended by two right angles, consisting of six signs and 180 degrees—and also those parts between which there is a "trine" length, containing one right angle and a third of another, consisting of four si... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "signa" (signs).</note>

...signs and one hundred and twenty degrees. Also, there are parts between which there is a square distance <note>original: "longitudo tetragona," referring to the 90-degree square aspect.</note>, which contain one right angle and consist of three signs and ninety degrees. Furthermore, there are parts between which there is a hexagonal distance <note>original: "hexagona," referring to the 60-degree sextile aspect.</note>, which encompass two-thirds of a right angle and consist of two signs and sixty degrees. We shall learn the reasons why we ought to observe only these distances and no others from what follows. Indeed, the reasons for observing the distance of a single diameter <note>original: "diametri," the 180-degree opposition aspect.</note> are self-evident, because the signs are stretched away from each other in a straight line. When we consider the two larger parts <note>The trine and the square/sextile ratios.</note>, in which there is a mathematical agreement between the part and the whole, these remaining figures are established. By the "agreement of the part," it works like this: when we assign a proportion to the distance of two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>, which is the length of the diameter, the square distance <note>90 degrees</note> is its half; and its third part is the hexagonal distance <note>60 degrees</note>. From this hexagonal distance doubled, the trine distance <note>120 degrees</note> is created. By the "agreement of the whole and the part," it happens when we create a proportion from the square distance to the two other distances between which it is positioned: the proportion of one will be <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio. In degrees, 90:60 is 3:2.</note> and the other <term>sesquitertial</term> <note>A 4:3 ratio. In degrees, 120:90 is 4:3.</note>. When we assign the proportion from the square to that which is less than it—the ratio of which is sesquialter—the hexagonal distance is produced. And when we assign the proportion to the larger one—the ratio of which is sesquitertial—we establish the trine distance. They have called the trine and hexagonal aspects "harmonious" <note>original: "conuenientes"</note> because they are composed of signs that agree in gender—that is, they are either all masculine or all feminine. However, those formed by the diameter or the square figure they called "discordant" <note>original: "disconuenientes"</note> because they are always found in a state of opposition between signs that would otherwise agree in gender.

### ON THE HIGH AND LOW SIGNS, WHICH ARE CALLED PRECEPTING AND OBEDIENT. Chapter 15.

The parts of the zodiac whose distance from any one and the same point of the equinoctial points <note>The points where the celestial equator and ecliptic intersect, marking the start of Spring and Autumn.</note> is equal are called "high" and "low" <note>Also known as "commanding" and "obeying" signs.</note>. These are signs whose rising and setting times are equal, because they are carried along equal circumferences of parallel circles relative to the equinoctial circle. Of these parts, those formed in the middle of the summer circle <note>The signs nearing the Summer Solstice.</note> are called "high" or "sublime"; those in the middle of the winter circle <note>The signs nearing the Winter Solstice.</note> are named "low." This is because when the Sun progresses through the middle of the summer circle, it makes the days longer than the nights; but when it illuminates the half of the winter circle, it demonstrates that the days are shorter than the nights.

### ON SIGNS THAT BEHOLD ONE ANOTHER AND ARE EQUAL IN POWER. Chapter 16.

They also say there are certain parts that are equal to other parts in "power" or "strength" <note>These are often called "Antiscia."</note> when their distance from either of the two tropic points <note>The Summer and Winter Solstice points.</note> is one and the same. This is because when the Sun has reached either of these two points, day is equal to day and night to night, and the length of the hours will be the same. They also say that these parts "behold" each other because of these shared conditions, and because each of them rises from the same parts of the horizon in the East and sets in those same parts in the West.

### ON CONTRADICTING SIGNS, BETWEEN WHICH THERE IS NO BOND. Chapter 17.

Indeed, those parts which are called "contradicting" or "alien" <note>Often called "Aversion" or "Inconjunct" signs.</note> are those between which none of the aforementioned affinities exist. That is, they are neither "precepting," nor "obedient," nor "beholding each other" with equal power. Nor are they among those which have an affinity through the positioning of the four geometric figures—the diameter, the trine, the square, and the hexagon. The parts which we find to be associated in no way by these methods are those between which one or five signs are contained <note>These represent the 30-degree and 150-degree distances.</note>. ### CHAPTER XVIII. ON THE HOUSES OF THE FIVE WANDERING STARS,
### and of the Sun and Moon.

The parts of the zodiac circle—which are called houses, triplicities, exaltations, and terms, and similar names—are assigned to the seven planets because they share some similarity or dignity with them. The nature of the "houses" <note>Also known as "domiciles," these are the signs where a planet is most "at home" and powerful.</note> is as follows. Since among the twelve signs, two are northern—namely those that are closest to the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note> of our heads and therefore generate the most heat, which are Cancer and Leo—they were attributed to the two greatest and most dignified luminaries as their houses. The sign of Leo, which is masculine, was established as the house of the Sun; the sign of Cancer, which is feminine, was established as the house of the Moon. Therefore, they called the half of the circle from Leo to Capricorn the "Solar half," and the other half from Aquarius to Cancer they called the "Lunar half." This was done so that in each of the two halves of the circle—the solar and the lunar—each of the planets would have a house suitable to itself, according to the order of their spheres and their natures.

<margin>The nature of Saturn.</margin> Therefore, because Saturn is naturally cold and contrary to heat, and its sphere is the highest and most remote from the luminaries, they assigned to it the two signs of Capricorn and Aquarius, which are in opposition to Cancer and Leo. This was because these two, Capricorn and Aquarius, are cold and wintry signs; and furthermore, the relationship of shapes formed by opposition is not favorable or fortunate.

<margin>Of Jupiter.</margin> But because Jupiter’s nature is temperate and it travels beneath the sphere of Saturn, the two signs following Capricorn and Aquarius—which are Sagittarius and Pisces—were attributed to it. This is because they produce winds and compel things to grow, and they are at a <term>trine</term> <note>A 120-degree aspect, considered very harmonious.</note> distance from the houses of the luminaries, which is a favorable and fortunate position.

<margin>Of Mars.</margin> After these, because Mars naturally dries things out and its sphere revolves beneath the sphere of Jupiter, they gave it the two signs located after Jupiter’s dwellings, which are Aries and Scorpio. Their distance from the houses of the luminaries is <term>quadrate</term> <note>A 90-degree "square" aspect.</note>, which is appropriate for a destructive and contradictory heat, matching the nature of Mars.

<margin>Of Venus.</margin> However, because the star of Venus is of a temperate nature and revolves beneath the sphere of Mars, the two signs following the dwellings of Mars were attributed to it: Taurus and Libra. These make things grow and are at a <term>sextile</term> <note>A 60-degree aspect, representing opportunity and friendship.</note> distance from the houses of the luminaries, which is a distance of similarity and agreement.

<margin>Of Mercury.</margin> And because Venus is also found to have two parts, it is never distant from the Sun by more than two signs. Likewise, since Mercury remained among the wandering stars—which in neither of its two parts is ever distant from the Sun by more than the space of one sign, and travels beneath the other stars—the two remaining signs were given to it, which are located after the places of the luminaries: Gemini and Virgo.

### CHAPTER XIX. ON THE TRIPLICITIES AND THEIR 
### LORDS.

The relationships of the <term>triplicities</term> <note>Groups of three signs forming a triangle, usually associated with the four elements.</note> with the planets are these. Because the shape of an equilateral triangle is equal and harmonious in itself, and because the three boundaries of the zodiac circle—namely the equinoctial circle and the two solstice circles—divided the twelve parts of the zodiac into four equilateral triangles. The first triplicity consists of Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, which are masculine signs; they are the homes of the Sun, Jupiter, and Mars. Therefore, they gave this triplicity to the Sun and Jupiter, rejecting Mars, because Mars is of a <term>haiz</term> <note>original: "haiz"; an Arabic term referring to a planet's "sect" or proper condition. Mars is a "night" planet and doesn't fit the "day" triplicity of the Sun.</note> contrary to the *haiz* of the Sun. The first lord of this triplicity by day is the Sun, but by night it is Jupiter. The sign of Aries also follows the equinoctial circle, Leo is closer to the summer circle, and Sagittarius stands nearer to the winter circle. This triplicity is also northern because Jupiter has dominion there. The sign of Aries follows the equinoctial circle, compels things to grow, and brings northern winds. Furthermore, because the house of Mars is in it, he is said to have a partnership there with the northern wind, and somewhat from the west...

The **second triplicity**, however, which is gathered from the three feminine signs—namely **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**—is assigned to the Moon and Venus, because it belongs to the <term>haiz</term> <note>original: *haiz*; an Arabic astrological term used here to describe a planet’s "sect" or its favorable condition when in a sign or position that matches its nature.</note> of the Moon. This triplicity produces western winds because of the dominion of Mars and the Moon within it; and because Venus is associated with it, the wind will be gathered from the west and the south.

### CHAPTER XX. ON EXALTATIONS.

The modes of the signs, which are called the **exaltations** <note>Signs where a planet’s influence is "raised" or amplified to its greatest potential.</note> of the luminaries and the wandering stars, are as I shall subjoin. For when the Sun is in the sign of **Aries**, it is moved toward the higher northern half of the circle. When it enters the sign of **Libra**, it turns its proper journey toward the lower southern half of the circle. For this reason, they established the sign of Aries—in which the length of the days and the increase of their natural heat begins—as the **exaltation** of the Sun. But Libra, because of the contrary nature of the aforementioned conditions, they declared to be its **fall** <note>original: *casus*; the sign opposite the exaltation where the planet's power is most weakened.</note>. Regarding Saturn, his distance from the Sun is one of opposition, just as in the houses; for where heat grows, coldness is diminished, and where coldness is intensified, heat is diminished. Thus, Saturn received the sign of Libra for his exaltation and Aries for his fall. Likewise, when the Moon is in the sign of Aries with the Sun (which is his exaltation), it will first appear [as a crescent] afterwards in **Taurus**, which is the beginning, as it were, of the increase of its light; therefore its exaltation was in Taurus, which is the first sign of its own triplicity. In the sign of **Scorpio**, however, which is formed in opposition to that, its fall is designated. And because Jupiter is the author of northern winds, which cause things to grow, and since his power appears most clearly when he is at his greatest northern declination (which is in **Cancer**) and produces northern winds, they granted the sign of Cancer as his exaltation and **Capricorn** as his fall. Mars, however, since he is naturally burning, and especially when he is in Capricorn—because his declination is then in the southern part—is "sublimated" <note>Exalted.</note> in Capricorn, which is contrary to the exaltation of Jupiter; he falls, however, in Cancer. Again, because Venus naturally moistens, especially in the sign of **Pisces**, in which the moisture of spring appears and its natural force begins to grow, she is exalted in Pisces and falls in **Virgo**. Mercury, however, since he dries things out, is exalted in the sign of Virgo in contrast to Venus; in which sign autumn, which...

## ON THE TERMS. CHAPTER 21.

There are two systems of **Terms** <note>original: *termini*; these are specific subdivisions of each zodiac sign, where different planets are said to have "bounds" or influence over specific degrees.</note>: one is called **Egyptian**, the other **Chaldean**. The one called Egyptian is primarily based on the **lords of the houses**; the Chaldean, however, is taken from the **lords of the triplicities**. But the Egyptian system does not truly change the order or the quantities of each, which is generally set as the root, according to the methods of the terms. For they assign the first in order to the lords of the houses, and sometimes to the lords of the triplicities, and sometimes to the lords of the exaltations. For example, in **Libra**, they do not start with **Venus**, but with **Saturn**; and in **Aries**, they did not start with **Mars**, but with **Jupiter**. If they followed the lords of the triplicities and no others, why in **Capricorn** did they take their beginning from **Mercury** and not from **Venus**? Likewise, if they followed the lords of the exaltations and no others, why in **Cancer** do they begin with **Mars** and not with **Jupiter**? Again, if in these cases they followed only the planets which have the most strengths among the aforementioned powers, why in **Aquarius** did they make the beginning with **Mercury**, who only has a triplicity there, and not with **Saturn**, who possesses both the house and the triplicity? In **Capricorn** also, they began with **Mercury**, who has no authority there. The order of the remaining terms is found in this same manner. 

In the quantities <note>The number of degrees assigned to each planet within a sign.</note> of the terms, they also seem to observe no order. For in the total number of all these terms, which is collected for each of the planets—which they announce to be of the same quantity as the number of years for that planet—there is no logic by which the length of life can be proved according to this. But even if we were to say and grant that the number collected from this is the true number, as is affirmed by the **Egyptians**, perhaps the same number would be collected even if the quantities of the terms were varied in many different ways. Some, however, who seem to affirm this point because it seems sufficient to them by physical reasoning, say that when the **times of ascension** <note>The time it takes for a portion of the zodiac to rise above the horizon.</note> of the terms of each planet have been collected, one and the same quantity will be produced from them in all climates <note>Latitudinal zones of the Earth.</note>. It is manifest that this is false. For in this, they have followed what is found in the **book of the foolish**, and they have used equal additions instead of true ascensions. No one doubts that this is contrary to the truth. For it is found in this book that the ascensions of **Virgo** and **Libra**, on the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator.</note> parallel to the line that passes through the lower parts of the region of **Egypt**, are 37 and a third times for each of the two aforementioned signs, and that the ascensions of each of the two signs, **Leo** and **Scorpio**, are 36 times. But by geometric reasoning it is proved that **Leo** and **Scorpio** rise in more than 35 times, while **Virgo** and **Libra** rise in less than the aforementioned times. 

Likewise, those who brought forward this reasoning did not follow those quantities of the terms which many people have affirmed. In many places, it is found necessary that they are lying. But so that their opinion might appear firmer, they divided the degrees into minutes; however, we do not declare them to be truthful for this reason, but most deceitful in this matter, as we said before. Their terms, which we criticize here for the aforementioned reasons, are those which they stated as follows below. Moreover, what is collected for each of these planets from the aforementioned degrees is this: for **Saturn** fifty-seven, for **Jupiter** 79, for **Mars** 66, for **Venus** 82, and for **Mercury** 76; the collection of all of these is 360 degrees.

But they reason through another method, which they have called the **Chaldean**, based on the lords of the **triplicities** <note>Groups of three signs belonging to the same element: Fire, Earth, Air, or Water.</note>: their reasoning is found to be both clearer and more sufficient; and yet they do not always follow the planets that rule the triplicities, neither in their order nor in their quantities. Their opinion, however, can be briefly committed to memory without a book. For in the **first triplicity**, which consists of **Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius**, the division of terms among them is one and the same in each of its signs. For they give the first term to the lord of the triplicity, which is **Jupiter**; the second to the lord of the following triplicity, which is **Venus**; the third and fourth to the two lords of the Gemini triplicity <note>Referring to the Air triplicity, of which Gemini is a member.</note>, which are **Saturn** and **Mercury**; and the fifth to the lord of the remaining triplicity, which is **Mars**.

But for the **second triplicity**, which is gathered from **Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn**, each of the signs is divided by one and the same arrangement: and they assign the first term to **Venus**, because of her lordship over it; the second and third to the two lords of the Gemini triplicity, who are **Saturn** and **Mercury**; after these, they assigned the fourth to **Mars**, and the remainder to **Jupiter**. They followed this order most especially in the two remaining triplicities, except that in the **third triplicity**, which is said to have two lords, namely **Saturn** and **Mercury**, **Saturn** takes the first part during the day, but **Mercury** at night. 

Moreover, the method for the quantity of the terms found in each sign, which follows the aforementioned order, is indeed singular and manifest: their quantities do not differ except by an equal decrease. For each of the terms is decreased in quantity by one degree from the one preceding it. For they set the first term of each sign at eight degrees, the second at seven, the third at six, the fourth at five, and the fifth at four, which completes the total of thirty degrees. From all of these, there are collected for **Saturn** 78 degrees in the day, but 66 at night; for **Jupiter** 72; for **Mars** 60; for **Venus** 75; and for **Mercury** 66 in the day, but 78 at night. 

But of these two systems, that which was stated by the Egyptians agrees more with the truth, because the authors of the Egyptian books compiled them from what they found recorded in **nativities** <note>original: *nativitates*; individual birth charts or horoscopes used as empirical evidence.</note>; they collected these and wrote them in their books, which they had arranged as an exemplary path of the degrees of the terms, in those [records]...

We, however, in a certain very ancient book—the greater part of which had been consumed by extreme age and was riddled with holes—found the terms, in which that which was contained regarding the order and quantity of times was arranged naturally and rationally. Likewise, in that book, we found the degrees of the aforementioned births <note>original: *natiuitatū*</note>, and how many degrees each one of the planets held; and it agreed with that which is found in the books of the ancients. There was also in it a very long discourse in which these terms were proved by many necessary arguments. But because of its extreme antiquity and the frequent holes in the leaves, we were unable to transcribe it, and all its reasonings seemed difficult and obscure to us. 

Nevertheless, the portions of the terms that helped us greatly in understanding these things remained intact and undamaged near the end of the book, and whatever we found there regarding the terms is added here. In the order, consideration was given in each of the signs to the lord of the exaltation, of the triplicity, and of the house <note>These are the "essential dignities," or ways a planet gains strength based on its position in the zodiac.</note>; and whichever of them had two of these powers <note>original: *poteštates*</note> in a sign—and if it were a fortunate planet <note>original: *in fortuna*; referring to the "benefics" Jupiter and Venus.</note>—it preceded in the order. Whichever planet held two powers in a sign was placed ahead in the order of one holding only one power. Except that in Leo and Cancer, which are the homes of the Sun and Moon <note>The luminaries are not assigned terms of their own.</note>, they assigned the first term of each sign to one of the unfortunate planets. For they gave the first term of Cancer to Mars, and the first of Leo to Saturn. The order of these two planets was maintained in these two signs because in all other signs they were placed last. Thus, the method for the quantity of the terms is this: when none of the planets were found to have two powers in the same sign, nor in the following signs up to the fourth sign, then if it were one of the two fortunes (which are Jupiter and Venus), they assigned seven degrees to it. ### ON THE TWELFTHS. CHAPTER XXII.

There are indeed some who have divided the signs into even shorter parts than those mentioned above, calling them "places" and "degrees." Specifically, they called a "place" the **twelfth part** <note>Known as *dodecatemoria*, these are 2.5-degree segments of a sign.</note> of a sign, which consists of two and a half degrees; they also assigned their rulers as the lords of the houses, according to the succession of the signs. Others, however, divided them by other parts—specifically by ten signs—and followed the same order that the Chaldeans followed in the order of the terms. But since their method is inconsistent, we believe it should be set aside. We shall instead follow another method which we ought to imitate, because it is consistent. In both the **twelfths** and the **terms**, we shall begin from the two equinoctial points and the two solstitial points, just as the authors of the books have explained. And since the forces of nature and their similarities are specifically perceived, they began from no other place than the two equinoctial and two solstitial points, as we have said before, nor did they have any occasion to begin from anywhere else. For if any other beginning besides these were to be found, it would necessarily follow either that nothing is permitted to advance in their nature toward the perfection of this science, or that it should be both permitted and observed to be useful in some way. If anyone admits otherwise, he will be deceived, because he will have failed to observe the parts of the circle of the signs through which these forces come about.

**T**he similarities of the wandering stars <note>original: *erraticarum stellarum*; the planets</note> to the signs are formed as

<columns>1</columns>

we have said before. Likewise, it is similarly shown that the planets properly possess *almugea* <note>A configuration where a planet’s distance from the Sun or Moon matches the distance between their respective ruling signs</note> when each of them has some association in figure with the Sun or Moon. This occurs in the manner called *almugea*; that is, that there be between each [planet] and the Sun or Moon a longitudinal distance equal to the distance between its own house and the house of the Sun or Moon. For example, if Venus were in a sextile aspect <note>an angle of 60 degrees</note> with either luminary, so that she was western to the Sun or eastern to the Moon, she would then be in *almugea*. This, therefore, is the mode of *almugea* for each of the planets with the luminaries. Following this is *alchinara* <note>from the Arabic *al-kanārā*, referring to a planet's appearance or "brightness" when in a favorable state</note>, which occurs when a planet is in its *haiz* <note>a technical term for a planet being in its "proper place" based on its gender, the sign's gender, and whether it is day or night</note>, and in similar agreeable locations. When any one of them has two or more authorities <note>dignities or claims of rulership</note> in a location, it is said to be in its place of "joy" and "honor," and their powers are then increased because they are likened to the signs in which they reside, which aids their strength. They are also said to "rejoice" even when they are not likened to the signs in the aforementioned way, but when the planets that are of their *haiz* are likened to those locations; though this similarity is very remote, it is nonetheless something. But when they are found in foreign places—namely, in a contrary *haiz*—their own powers greatly decrease, and then their temperaments <note>original: *complexiones*; the mixture of qualities like heat or moisture</note> are contrary to the temperament of the signs in which they reside. For this reason, the resulting effect will be a combination of two different natures.

**BOOK TWO.**

### ON APPLICATION, AND SEPARATION, AND other virtues. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>that is, application.</margin>
The general rule of this chapter is that planets which precede, and those which seek the conjunction of others, are considered to be in [aspect] with one of them, unless there is a great distance between them which is larger than the sum of the half-diameters of the two planetary bodies. This occurs if it is from a conjunction or from any of the aforementioned configurations <note>Ptolemy refers to the "aspects": conjunction, sextile, square, trine, and opposition</note>. For this reason, it is useful to consider the latitude of their conjunction. Similarly, it is also helpful in such significations to consider the latitude of their conjunction. However, in any of the other configurations, observing this is unnecessary, because all their rays always extend to the center of the earth, and there they join from every side. It is also manifest from what has been said that the powers of all planets must be investigated from their own natures, and from the signs, as well as from the configurations they have in relation to the Sun, and also the <term>angles</term> <note>The "angles" are the four most powerful points in a chart: the Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli.</note> according to all the aforementioned methods. Regarding the quantity of their power, we should know that when they are <term>oriental</term> <note>Rising before the Sun.</note> and their own motion is increasing, they will be as strong as they can be. And when their motion is diminished and they are <term>occidental</term> <note>Setting after the Sun.</note>, they will be as weak as they can be. The same also happens to them according to the quality of their <term>horizons</term>. For when they are in the Midheaven, or when they have ascended to the Midheaven, they will be very strong; but they gradually decline from strength according to their distance from the Midheaven. For when they are at the very eastern point of the horizon (the Ascendant), they will not be as strong, and at the western point even less so. And when they are beneath the earth in opposition to the Midheaven, or between the west and the <term>angle of the earth</term> <note>The Imum Coeli, the lowest point of the chart.</note>, they will be even less strong. Similarly, they are said to be strong when, not by this but by another configuration, they have some association with the <term>Ascendant</term>. But when none of these are present, they will be weak and thought to have no strength.

## BOOK II.

### ON THE GENERAL DIVISION OF THIS science. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'E' within a woodcut border illustrating a landscape with buildings and mountains.</image-desc>
THOSE things, therefore, in which the foundations have been laid, and which one ought to use for the inquiry into particular prognostications, those things which have been generally presented by us, are sufficient. Now, however, as the discourse is continuous, the particulars which they may grasp by this method of prognosticating should be added after what has been said, in which we shall follow a direct path agreeable to natural things. We shall say, therefore, because the prediction of the stars is divided into two parts, which are its greater and more powerful parts: the first and that which is universal, is that part concerning what shall happen in regions and lands, and it is called the "Universal" part. The second part, which is less universal than the former, is that which discerns what shall happen to each individual, and it is named the "Science of Nativities" <note>Also known as Genethlialogy.</note>. I have thought it worthy to present the Universal part first, because this universal part is altered by occasions which are said to be stronger and greater than those of individuals. Wherefore, because weak natures are contained under stronger ones, and particulars under universals in all their qualities, it is necessary that those who seek to observe particulars should hasten to observe first those things which are more universal and of greater consequence. And since from these universal observations, some indicate the general state of regions, while others indicate the general state of lands—certain major and general afflictions, such as wars, deaths, famines, earthquakes, floods, and similar things—others demonstrate smaller afflictions than those aforementioned, which happen at certain hours, such as the years, the changes of seasons, the increases of heat and cold and winds, and their decreases, their intensities and remissions, the abundance of rains, and droughts, and similar things. And because that which precedes from these two parts is the science of those things which shall generally happen in regions, and of great afflictions, because of the aforementioned occasions. In the knowledge of these things we properly use two methods, one of which is the similarity of the signs and stars in each <term>climate</term> <note>Ancient geography divided the world into "climates" or latitudinal zones.</note>; the other is the signs occurring at specific hours and times, and in similar parts, according to the Moon and...

### ON THE UNIVERSAL CHARACTERISTICS OF THE CLIMATES. Chapter II.

<margin>Northern inhabitants.</margin>
There are indeed certain characteristics of nations which occur generally according to the parallel lines and the angles of the earth, because of their similarities with the circle of the signs <note>the Zodiac</note> and with the Sun. For since that part of the earth in which we are supported is in one of the two northern quarters, for those who dwell in it under the parallel lines closest to the south—which are the lines extending between the summer solstice point and the equinoctial point—the Sun runs through the <term>zenith</term> <note>the point directly overhead</note> of their heads and scorches them. Therefore, their bodies are black, and their hair is black and curly with a rough texture; their faces are parched, and their bodies are lean. Their natures are also hot, and the qualities of their souls are for the most part cruel <note>Ptolemy follows the ancient theory that extreme climate dictates temperament; extreme heat was thought to make the "spirit" fierce or wild.</note>, because of the long and constant stay of the Sun in their regions.
<margin>Ethiopians.</margin>
And these are they who are generally called Ethiopians by others. It is not only in these people that this quality of heat appears, but even in the surrounding air; a fierce heat is detected in all animals and in the plants that exist among them.
<margin>† Otherwise the Bear.</margin>
However, in those who dwell under the parallel lines closer to the North—that is, those who live in places situated under the <term>Enatnam</term> <note>original: "Enatnã"; a reference to the constellation Ursa Major, or the Big Dipper</note>—because their distance from the circle of the signs is great, cold overcomes the heat of the Sun. For this reason, because their humidity is great and they have much vegetation, and there is no heat among them to dry it out, their complexions are white and their hair is straight; their bodies are large and fleshy, and their natures as well as their habits are cold. Similarly, they are fierce because of the long and constant stay of the cold in their dwellings. Also, according to the quality of these things, there is a wintry quality in their air, and there is great size in their herbs.
<margin>Slavs.</margin>
